uses: Prevention of MI and stroke (primary & secondary)
CV risk reduction in type 2 diabetes
dA: Start 10–20 mg PO once daily, any time of day
Usual range 10–80 mg once daily
High-intensity (post-ACS, high risk): 40–80 mg daily
With strong CYP3A4 inhibitors: cap at 20 mg/day
dP: Heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia, age 10–17: 10 mg once daily; range 10–20 mg
dur: Long-term, usually lifelong. Keep taking even when feeling well.
hl: ~14 h (effect lasts 20–30 h via active metabolites)
se: Muscle pain/myopathy — rarely rhabdomyolysis with kidney injury
ix: Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (clarithromycin, itraconazole, ritonavir) — ↑levels, myopathy; cap 20 mg
Cyclosporine — greatly ↑exposure; avoid
Gemfibrozil — high rhabdo risk; avoid
Grapefruit juice (large amounts) — ↑levels
preg: Generally avoided in pregnancy — stop when pregnancy is recognized. Not recommended while breastfeeding.

boxed: Fetal toxicity: can injure or kill the fetus in the 2nd/3rd trimester — stop as soon as pregnancy is detected.
dA: HTN: start 10 mg PO once daily (5 mg if on a diuretic); usual 20–40 mg; max 80 mg/day
Heart failure: start 2.5–5 mg daily; titrate to max 40 mg
Acute MI: 5 mg within 24 h, then 5 mg at 24 h, 10 mg at 48 h, then 10 mg daily
dP: HTN, age ≥6: start 0.07 mg/kg once daily (max 5 mg); not for GFR <30
dur: Usually long-term/lifelong; ≥6 weeks after MI, often indefinitely.
ix: K+ supplements / K-sparing diuretics (spironolactone) — hyperkalemia
Sacubitril/valsartan — contraindicated; angioedema (36-h washout)
Lithium — ↑levels & toxicity
NSAIDs — ↓effect & kidney injury
Aliskiren — avoid dual RAS blockade
preg: Contraindicated in pregnancy (boxed warning) — fetal renal failure, oligohydramnios, death. Not recommended while breastfeeding.

boxed: Fetal toxicity — can injure or kill the fetus; stop as soon as pregnancy is detected.
uses: Stroke risk reduction in HTN with LVH
HF alternative when ACE inhibitors not tolerated
dA: HTN: 50 mg PO once daily; range 25–100 mg/day in 1–2 doses
Start 25 mg if volume-depleted or hepatic impairment
Diabetic nephropathy: 50 mg once daily, up to 100 mg
Full effect may take 3–6 weeks
dP: HTN, age ≥6: 0.7 mg/kg once daily (max 50 mg); not for GFR <30
dur: Long-term, usually lifelong.
ix: K+ supplements / K-sparing diuretics — hyperkalemia
Lithium — ↑levels & toxicity
NSAIDs — blunted BP effect, renal risk
Aliskiren — contraindicated in diabetes
Dual RAS blockade (ACEi/other ARB) — hypotension, hyperkalemia
preg: Contraindicated in pregnancy (boxed warning). Breastfeeding generally not recommended.

dA: HTN: 5 mg PO once daily; range 2.5–10 mg (max 10 mg/day)
Elderly/frail or hepatic impairment: start 2.5 mg
Angina/CAD: 5–10 mg once daily
Titrate every 7–14 days
dP: HTN, age 6–17: 2.5–5 mg once daily (max 5 mg/day)
dur: Long-term (often lifelong) daily therapy.
ix: Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (clarithromycin, ketoconazole) — ↑levels
Simvastatin — cap at 20 mg/day (myopathy)
Cyclosporine / tacrolimus — ↑levels, monitor
Other antihypertensives / nitrates — additive hypotension
preg: Limited data; crosses placenta. Use only if benefit outweighs risk. Small amounts in breast milk, no adverse effects reported.

boxed: Do not stop abruptly — sudden discontinuation can trigger angina, MI, or arrhythmia. Taper over 1–2 weeks.
uses: Heart failure with reduced EF (succinate ER)
dA: HTN (tartrate IR): 100 mg/day in 1–2 doses; max 450 mg/day
HTN (succinate ER): 25–100 mg once daily; max 400 mg/day
Heart failure (succinate ER only): start 12.5–25 mg daily, double q2 weeks to target 200 mg
Acute MI (tartrate): 5 mg IV q2min ×3, then 50 mg PO q6h
dP: HTN, age ≥6 (succinate ER): 1 mg/kg once daily (max 50 mg); up to 2 mg/kg
dur: Usually long-term/indefinite. Never stop abruptly — taper over 1–2 weeks.
ix: CYP2D6 inhibitors (fluoxetine, paroxetine, bupropion) — ↑levels, bradycardia
Verapamil / diltiazem — additive AV block
Clonidine — rebound HTN if clonidine stopped; stop metoprolol first
Digoxin — additive AV slowing
preg: Use only if benefit justifies risk; may cause fetal/neonatal bradycardia & hypoglycemia. Generally compatible with breastfeeding (monitor infant).

boxed: Potent diuretic — excessive doses cause profound diuresis with water/electrolyte depletion; requires careful supervision.
dA: Edema: 20–80 mg PO once daily; may ↑by 20–40 mg q6–8h; max 600 mg/day
HTN: 40 mg PO twice daily
Acute pulmonary edema: 40 mg IV over 1–2 min; may ↑to 80 mg IV
IV dose ≈ half the equivalent PO dose
dP: Edema: 2 mg/kg PO once; may ↑by 1–2 mg/kg q6–8h; IV 1 mg/kg/dose
dur: Often long-term for chronic HF/edema; short courses for acute overload.
ix: NSAIDs — blunt effect, kidney injury
Lithium — ↓clearance, toxicity
Aminoglycosides / cisplatin — additive oto/nephrotoxicity
Digoxin — hypokalemia ↑digoxin toxicity
preg: Use only if clearly needed. Passes into breast milk and may suppress lactation.

dA: Heart failure: 25 mg PO once daily; up to 50 mg
HTN: 25–100 mg/day in 1–2 doses
Edema (cirrhosis): 100 mg/day (range 25–200 mg)
Reduce frequency if eGFR 30–50
dP: Off-label: 1–3.3 mg/kg/day divided 1–2×
dur: Usually long-term chronic therapy.
ix: ACE inhibitors / ARBs — severe hyperkalemia
K+ supplements / other K-sparing diuretics — hyperkalemia
Trimethoprim (incl. TMP-SMX) — hyperkalemia
NSAIDs — ↓effect, hyperkalemia, renal injury
Lithium — ↓clearance, toxicity
preg: Avoid — anti-androgen effects may feminize a male fetus. Active metabolite in breast milk considered clinically inconsequential.

boxed: Bleeding risk — can cause major or fatal bleeding. Monitor INR regularly; watch for drug/diet/illness interactions.
uses: Treatment & prevention of DVT and PE
After MI to reduce recurrent events
dA: Initial: 2–5 mg PO once daily (lower in elderly/liver disease)
Maintenance: 2–10 mg once daily, adjusted to INR
Target INR 2.0–3.0 for VTE, AF, aortic mechanical valve
Target INR 2.5–3.5 for mitral mechanical valve
dP: No controlled pediatric studies; ~0.1 mg/kg/day start with frequent INR monitoring
dur: 3–6 months for a provoked clot; often indefinite for AF, recurrent VTE, mechanical valves.
ix: NSAIDs / aspirin / antiplatelets — ↑bleeding
Many antibiotics & azoles (TMP-SMX, metronidazole, fluconazole) — ↑INR
Amiodarone — ↑INR
Rifampin, carbamazepine — ↓effect, clot risk
Vitamin K–rich foods — ↓effect
preg: Contraindicated in pregnancy (embryopathy, fetal bleeding), except some mechanical-valve patients. Compatible with breastfeeding.

boxed: Stopping early (without alternative anticoagulation) ↑thrombotic events.
Spinal/epidural hematoma with neuraxial anesthesia — may cause permanent paralysis.
dA: Nonvalvular AF: 5 mg PO twice daily
Reduce to 2.5 mg BID if ≥2 of: age ≥80, ≤60 kg, creatinine ≥1.5
DVT/PE: 10 mg BID ×7 days, then 5 mg BID
Recurrent VTE prevention: 2.5 mg BID after ≥6 months
dP: Pediatric VTE (from birth, ≥2.6 kg): weight-tiered 0.3–10 mg BID after parenteral anticoagulation
dur: ≥3–6 months for VTE; ongoing/indefinite for AF; 12–35 days after joint replacement.
ix: Strong dual CYP3A4+P-gp inhibitors (ketoconazole, ritonavir) — halve dose or avoid
Strong dual inducers (rifampin, carbamazepine, phenytoin) — ↓effect; avoid
Other anticoagulants — additive bleeding
Antiplatelets / NSAIDs / aspirin — ↑bleeding
SSRIs/SNRIs — ↑bleeding
preg: May cause maternal/fetal bleeding; not first-line. Breastfeeding not recommended.

dA: VTE (weight-based drip): 80 units/kg IV bolus, then 18 units/kg/h, titrated to aPTT/anti-Xa
ACS: 60 units/kg bolus (max 4000), then 12 units/kg/h (max 1000/h)
SQ prophylaxis: 5000 units SQ q8–12h
Reversal: protamine sulfate
dP: Neonates/infants: 75–100 units/kg IV bolus, then 25–30 units/kg/h
Children: 75–100 units/kg bolus, then 18–20 units/kg/h (titrate)
dur: Short-term inpatient — usually days, until transitioned to oral anticoagulant or LMWH.
se: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) — immune platelet drop with paradoxical clotting; can occur weeks after stopping
ix: Warfarin / other anticoagulants — additive bleeding (expected during overlap)
Antiplatelets (aspirin, clopidogrel, NSAIDs) — ↑bleeding
Thrombolytics — major hemorrhage risk
Nitroglycerin IV — possible heparin resistance
preg: Does not cross the placenta — preferred anticoagulant class in pregnancy (use preservative-free). Minimal transfer to breast milk.

boxed: Reserve for life-threatening arrhythmias; load in hospital.
Pulmonary toxicity (up to 17%; can be fatal).
Hepatotoxicity — can be severe/fatal.
Proarrhythmia — can worsen or provoke arrhythmias incl. torsades.
dA: Cardiac arrest (VF/pulseless VT): 300 mg IV/IO push; may repeat 150 mg
VT with pulse: 150 mg IV over 10 min, then 1 mg/min ×6 h, then 0.5 mg/min ×18 h
Oral loading: 800–1600 mg/day ×1–3 weeks, then 600–800 mg/day ×1 month
Oral maintenance: usually 400 mg/day
dP: Cardiac arrest (PALS): 5 mg/kg IV/IO; may repeat (max 300 mg/dose). Not FDA-approved <18 yr.
dur: Often long-term daily; IV typically 1–3 days bridged to oral.
ix: Warfarin — potentiated; cut warfarin dose ⅓–½
Digoxin — ↑levels; reduce dose
Beta-blockers / verapamil / diltiazem — bradycardia & AV block
Other QT-prolonging drugs — torsades
Simvastatin — myopathy/rhabdo
preg: Can cause fetal harm (neonatal bradycardia, hypothyroidism); avoid unless no alternative. Breastfeeding not recommended.

boxed: Extravasation causes tissue ischemia/necrosis — infiltrate promptly with phentolamine.
dA: Start 8–12 mcg/min IV (~0.05–0.1 mcg/kg/min); titrate to MAP ≥65
Usual maintenance 2–4 mcg/min; much higher often needed in refractory shock
Give via central line when possible; never IV push
dP: Shock (PALS, off-label): 0.05–0.1 mcg/kg/min IV, titrate (up to ~2 mcg/kg/min)
dur: Continuous infusion for hours to days; wean as shock resolves.
ix: MAO inhibitors / linezolid — severe prolonged hypertension
Tricyclic antidepressants — exaggerated pressor response
Halogenated anesthetics — ventricular arrhythmias
Nonselective beta-blockers — unopposed alpha, severe HTN
preg: Do not withhold for life-threatening maternal hypotension. Breast-milk exposure unlikely clinically relevant.

dA: Anaphylaxis: 0.3–0.5 mg IM (1 mg/mL) in the thigh; repeat q5–10 min
Cardiac arrest: 1 mg IV/IO (0.1 mg/mL) q3–5 min
Shock: 0.05–2 mcg/kg/min IV, titrate to MAP
Severe asthma: 0.3–0.5 mg IM/SC
dP: Anaphylaxis: 0.01 mg/kg IM (max 0.3–0.5 mg), repeat q5–10 min
Cardiac arrest (PALS): 0.01 mg/kg IV/IO q3–5 min (max 1 mg)
dur: Single emergency doses; infusions run hours–days in shock.
ix: MAO inhibitors — dangerous potentiated pressor effect
Tricyclic antidepressants — exaggerated HTN/arrhythmias
Nonselective beta-blockers — severe HTN & blunted anaphylaxis response
Halogenated anesthetics — ventricular arrhythmias
preg: Use without hesitation in life-threatening maternal anaphylaxis/arrest. Compatible with breastfeeding.

dA: Induction: 2–2.5 mg/kg IV (1–1.5 if elderly/debilitated)
ICU sedation: start 5 mcg/kg/min, titrate 5–50 mcg/kg/min (avoid >4 mg/kg/h — PRIS)
Procedural: 100–150 mcg/kg/min ×3–5 min, then 25–75 mcg/kg/min
Requires airway/hemodynamic monitoring
dP: Induction (≥3 yr): 2.5–3.5 mg/kg IV. NOT for pediatric ICU sedation (deaths reported).
dur: Single induction doses; ICU infusions hours–days. Discard opened vial/tubing within 12 h.
hl: Clinical effect wears off in minutes (rapid redistribution)
se: Propofol infusion syndrome (acidosis, rhabdo, hyperK, cardiac failure)
ix: Opioids & benzodiazepines — additive sedation & cardiorespiratory depression
Valproate — ↑propofol levels; reduce dose
Antihypertensives / vasodilators — profound hypotension
Other CNS depressants (alcohol) — deeper sedation
preg: Crosses placenta; can cause neonatal sedation/respiratory depression. Small amounts in breast milk, no adverse effects reported.

dA: IV induction: 1–4.5 mg/kg slowly over ≥60 s (typical 1–2 mg/kg)
IM induction: 6.5–13 mg/kg
Maintenance: ½–full induction dose as needed
Analgesia: 0.1–0.3 mg/kg IV or low-dose infusion
dP: Label: safety not established <16 yr. Off-label procedural sedation: 1–2 mg/kg IV or 4–5 mg/kg IM.
dur: Single doses / brief infusions; anesthesia ~5–10 min per IV dose, recovery 1–2 h.
se: Emergence reactions — hallucinations, vivid dreams, delirium
ix: Theophylline/aminophylline — lowers seizure threshold; avoid
Opioids & CNS depressants — profound sedation/respiratory depression
Sympathomimetics — exaggerated HTN/tachycardia
Benzodiazepines — prolong recovery (but blunt emergence)
preg: Not recommended in pregnancy/obstetrics — animal fetal neurotoxicity. Brief breastfeeding interruption after a dose is reasonable.

boxed: Pediatric risk: acute rhabdomyolysis with hyperkalemia, cardiac arrest, and death in children with undiagnosed myopathy (esp. boys ≤8 yr) — reserve pediatric use for emergency airway.
dA: RSI: 1–1.5 mg/kg IV — paralysis in ~45–60 s
Short procedures: 0.3–1.1 mg/kg IV
No IV access: 3–4 mg/kg IM (max 150 mg)
dP: Emergency intubation only: infants/small children 2 mg/kg IV; older children 1 mg/kg IV
dur: Ultra-short: paralysis ~4–6 min after a single IV dose.
se: Life-threatening hyperkalemia (burns, crush injury, denervation, myopathy)
ix: Volatile inhaled anesthetics — potentiate block & MH risk
Cholinesterase inhibitors — prolonged paralysis
Aminoglycosides — enhanced/prolonged block
Magnesium & lithium — enhanced block
preg: Decades of use without identified fetal risk; used at cesarean (minimal placental transfer). Low risk in lactation (rapid breakdown).

boxed: Paralyzing agent — causes respiratory arrest; fatal without ventilatory support. Trained personnel & airway equipment required.
uses: Paralysis for RSI (non-depolarizing alternative to succinylcholine)
dA: RSI: 0.6–1.2 mg/kg IV (1.2 mg/kg fastest onset, ~60 s)
Standard intubation: 0.6 mg/kg IV (onset ~1 min, duration ~30 min)
Maintenance: 0.1–0.2 mg/kg IV as needed
Infusion: start 10–12 mcg/kg/min, titrate to twitch monitor
dP: Intubation: 0.45–0.6 mg/kg IV. Not recommended for RSI in children per label.
dur: Intermediate: ~30 min at 0.6 mg/kg; 60+ min after 1.2 mg/kg. Reversible with sugammadex.
ix: Volatile inhaled anesthetics — potentiate & prolong block
Aminoglycosides — enhanced block
Magnesium & lithium — enhanced block
Chronic carbamazepine/phenytoin — resistance, shorter block
Sugammadex — rapidly reverses rocuronium
preg: Use only if benefit justifies risk; not recommended for RSI at cesarean. No human milk data.

uses: Quick relief of acute bronchospasm in asthma (rescue)
dA: HFA inhaler (90 mcg/puff): 2 puffs q4–6h PRN
Exercise-induced: 2 puffs 15–30 min before exercise
Nebulizer: 2.5 mg q4–6h (may repeat q20 min ×3 in acute severe attacks)
dP: HFA (age ≥4): 2 puffs q4–6h PRN
Nebulizer (2–12 yr): 1.25–2.5 mg q4–6h
dur: Works in minutes; lasts ~4–6 h. Used as needed, not on a fixed schedule.
ix: Beta-blockers — block bronchodilation, may trigger severe bronchospasm
MAO inhibitors / tricyclics — potentiate CV effects
Loop/thiazide diuretics — worsened hypokalemia
Digoxin — albuterol may lower levels
preg: Standard rescue agent, generally continued in pregnancy. Low systemic levels make breastfeeding acceptable.

dA: Asthma (age ≥12): Diskus 100/50, 250/50, or 500/50 — 1 inhalation twice daily
Asthma HFA: 2 inhalations twice daily
COPD: Diskus 250/50 — 1 inhalation twice daily
Rinse mouth after use to prevent thrush
dP: Asthma, 4–11 yr: Diskus 100/50 — 1 inhalation twice daily
dur: Daily controller, twice daily; ~12 h per dose. Full effect over days–weeks.
se: Adrenal suppression & growth slowing in children (high doses)
ix: Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (ritonavir, ketoconazole) — marked ↑exposure; avoid
MAO inhibitors / tricyclics — potentiated CV effects
Beta-blockers — block bronchodilation
Loop/thiazide diuretics — additive hypokalemia
Other LABAs — do not combine
preg: Weigh against the real harm of uncontrolled asthma. Expected low milk levels; generally compatible with breastfeeding.

boxed: Serious neuropsychiatric events — agitation, depression, sleep disturbance, and suicidal thoughts/behavior. Reserve for allergic rhinitis only if other therapies fail.
dA: Asthma or allergic rhinitis (age ≥15): 10 mg PO once daily (evening for asthma)
Exercise-induced: 10 mg at least 2 h before exercise; no repeat within 24 h
dP: 6–14 yr: 5 mg chewable once daily (evening)
2–5 yr: 4 mg chewable or granules once daily
12–23 months (asthma): 4 mg granules once daily
dur: Ongoing daily controller (evening); not for an acute attack.
se: Neuropsychiatric events (agitation, aggression, depression, suicidality, vivid dreams)
ix: Phenobarbital — ↓montelukast levels
Rifampin — ↓levels; monitor response
Gemfibrozil — ↑exposure several-fold
Phenytoin — reduced effect possible
preg: Registry/cohort data show no clear ↑in birth defects; often continued for asthma. Limited milk data — use caution.

boxed: Lactic acidosis: rare but potentially fatal; risk ↑ with renal impairment (contraindicated eGFR <30), age >65, liver disease, hypoxia, heavy alcohol, iodinated contrast.
dA: IR: 500 mg PO twice daily or 850 mg once daily with meals
Titrate by 500 mg weekly; usual 2000 mg/day; max 2550 mg/day
ER: 500–1000 mg once daily with evening meal; max 2000 mg/day
Do not start if eGFR 30–45; hold for iodinated contrast if risk factors
dP: Age ≥10 (IR): 500 mg PO twice daily; titrate weekly; max 2000 mg/day
dur: Long-term, often lifelong.
hl: ~6.2 h plasma (~17.6 h whole blood); prolonged in renal impairment
se: Diarrhea, nausea, abdominal discomfort (common, usually transient)
ix: Iodinated contrast — hold metformin (AKI & lactic acidosis risk)
Alcohol (heavy/binge) — potentiates lactic acidosis
Topiramate / acetazolamide — ↑lactic acidosis risk
Cimetidine — ↑metformin levels
Insulin / sulfonylureas — additive hypoglycemia
preg: Widely used in pregnancy, though insulin often preferred. Small amounts in breast milk — discuss with provider.

boxed: Thyroid C-cell tumor risk in rodents; human relevance unknown. Contraindicated with personal/family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma or MEN 2.
uses: CV risk reduction in T2DM / obesity with CVD
dA: Ozempic (SC weekly): 0.25 mg ×4 wk → 0.5 mg → up to 1 mg → max 2 mg
Wegovy (SC weekly): escalate q4 wk to 2.4 mg maintenance
Rybelsus (PO daily): 3 mg ×30 days → 7 mg → max 14 mg, fasting with ≤4 oz water
0.25 mg start is for GI tolerability, not glucose control
dP: Wegovy: chronic weight management age 12+, titrate to 2.4 mg weekly. Ozempic/Rybelsus not approved in children.
dur: Long-term; weight regain / glucose worsening common after stopping.
ix: Insulin — ↑hypoglycemia; reduce insulin dose
Sulfonylureas — ↑hypoglycemia
Oral drugs — delayed gastric emptying may alter absorption (warfarin, levothyroxine)
Other GLP-1 agonists — do not combine
preg: Not recommended; stop ≥2 months before a planned pregnancy (long half-life). Avoid while breastfeeding.

uses: Basal insulin for type 1 diabetes (with mealtime insulin)
Once-daily glycemic control when orals insufficient
dA: T1DM: ~⅓ of total daily insulin SC once daily (total need ~0.4–1 units/kg/day); pair with rapid-acting
T2DM (insulin-naive): 0.2 units/kg (up to 10 units) SC once daily, then titrate to fasting glucose
Toujeo U-300: titrate no more often than q3–4 days
Give at the same time each day; never mix in a syringe
dP: Age ≥6 (T1DM): ~⅓ of total daily insulin (~0.2–0.4 units/kg/day initial)
dur: Daily long-term; lifelong in type 1 diabetes.
hl: No pronounced peak; flat ~24 h profile (Toujeo up to 36 h)
se: Peripheral edema; HF when combined with TZDs
ix: Other antidiabetics & ACE inhibitors — additive hypoglycemia
Thiazolidinediones — fluid retention, HF risk
Beta-blockers, clonidine — mask hypoglycemia warning signs
Corticosteroids, thiazides, atypical antipsychotics — ↑glucose
Alcohol — unpredictable glucose effects
preg: Insulin is standard in pregnancy; no clear fetal-harm signal. Compatible with breastfeeding.

dA: Inject SC within 15 min before or right after a meal
Typically 50–65% basal / remainder as lispro across meals
Total daily insulin commonly 0.4–1 units/kg/day (basal + bolus)
U-100 and U-200 pens deliver same units — do not convert
dP: Approved age 3+; individualized units/kg; often 0.4–1 units/kg/day (higher in puberty)
dur: Daily long-term with every meal; lifelong in type 1 diabetes.
hl: ~1 h SC; onset ~15 min, peak 30–90 min, lasts 2–4 h
ix: Other hypoglycemics & ACE inhibitors — additive hypoglycemia
Thiazolidinediones — fluid retention, HF risk
Beta-blockers — mask hypoglycemia symptoms
Corticosteroids, thiazides, sympathomimetics — ↑glucose
Alcohol — unpredictable swings
preg: Insulin preferred in pregnancy; lispro widely used. Compatible with breastfeeding.

boxed: Not for obesity/weight loss — ineffective and larger doses can cause serious or life-threatening toxicity, especially with sympathomimetic appetite suppressants.
uses: TSH suppression in differentiated thyroid cancer
dA: ~1.6 mcg/kg PO once daily on an empty stomach, 30–60 min before breakfast
Age >50 or cardiac disease: start 12.5–25 mcg; ↑q6–8 weeks
Recheck TSH q4–6 weeks until stable
Separate from interfering meds/food by ≥4 h
dP: 0–3 mo: 10–15 mcg/kg/day; 1–5 yr: 5–6 mcg/kg/day; >12 yr (growth complete): ~1.6 mcg/kg/day
Congenital hypothyroidism: start promptly
dur: Usually lifelong replacement.
se: Over-replacement thyrotoxicosis: palpitations, tremor, heat intolerance, insomnia, weight loss
ix: Calcium, iron, antacids, cholestyramine, sucralfate — block absorption; separate by 4 h
PPIs — reduced absorption
Warfarin — enhanced anticoagulant effect; monitor INR
Estrogens — may ↑levothyroxine requirement
Insulin/orals — may need dose adjustment
preg: Safe and essential in pregnancy — requirements often ↑, check TSH each trimester. Compatible with breastfeeding.

dA: General anti-inflammatory: 5–60 mg PO daily, individualized
Asthma/COPD burst: 40–60 mg daily ×3–10 days (no taper for short courses)
Chronic disease: lowest effective dose; taper if used >~2 weeks
dP: Anti-inflammatory: 0.5–2 mg/kg/day
Asthma exacerbation: 1–2 mg/kg/day (max 60 mg) ×3–10 days
dur: Short bursts of 3–10 days for flares; weeks–months (with taper) for chronic disease.
hl: Plasma ~2–3 h; biologic effect 18–36 h (once-daily dosing)
se: Insomnia & mood changes (psychosis at high doses)
ix: NSAIDs / aspirin — additive GI ulcer/bleed
Live vaccines — avoid (disseminated infection, poor response)
Warfarin — altered INR; monitor
CYP3A4 inducers (rifampin, phenytoin) — ↓steroid effect
Insulin/orals — steroid raises glucose
preg: Use only if benefit justifies risk; largely inactivated by placenta. Compatible with breastfeeding at low–moderate doses.

dA: Anti-inflammatory: 0.75–9 mg PO/IV/IM daily
Cerebral edema: 10 mg IV once, then 4 mg q6h; taper over 5–7 days
CINV: 12–20 mg before chemo, then 8 mg daily ×2–4 days
Taper if therapy lasts more than a few days
dP: Croup: 0.6 mg/kg PO/IM/IV ×1 (max 16 mg)
Cerebral edema: 0.2 mg/kg/24 h divided
dur: Often a single dose (croup) or a few days; longer courses need a taper.
hl: Plasma ~4 h; biologic effect 36–72 h (longest-acting common steroid)
ix: NSAIDs / aspirin — additive GI bleed
Live vaccines — avoid
CYP3A4 inducers (rifampin, phenytoin) — ↓levels; dexamethasone also lowers levels of many drugs
Warfarin — altered INR
Insulin/orals — worsened glycemic control
preg: Crosses the placenta; use only if benefit justifies risk. Appears in breast milk — weigh risk vs benefit.

dA: GERD: 20 mg PO once daily ×4 weeks (up to 8 for erosive esophagitis)
Duodenal ulcer: 20 mg daily ×4–8 weeks; H. pylori: 20 mg BID with antibiotics ×10–14 days
Take 30–60 min before a meal
OTC course is 14 days
dP: GERD (age 1–16): 10 to <20 kg: 10 mg daily; ≥20 kg: 20 mg daily
dur: Typically 4–8 weeks; long-term only for maintenance/hypersecretory states.
hl: Plasma 0.5–1 h, but acid suppression up to 72 h (once-daily)
ix: Clopidogrel — avoid; omeprazole ↓its activation, ↓antiplatelet effect
Rilpivirine — contraindicated
High-dose methotrexate — ↑levels/toxicity
Acid-dependent drugs (ketoconazole, atazanavir, iron) — ↓absorption
Warfarin — ↑INR; monitor
preg: Human data do not show ↑birth-defect risk; acceptable when needed. May be present in breast milk — weigh benefit vs risk.

uses: Upper GI bleed / stress ulcer prophylaxis (IV, common inpatient use)
dA: Erosive esophagitis: 40 mg PO once daily up to 8 weeks
Maintenance: 40 mg daily
Zollinger-Ellison: 40 mg BID, titrate (max 240 mg/day)
GI bleed (off-label): 80 mg IV bolus then infusion, or 40–80 mg IV
dP: Erosive esophagitis (age ≥5): 15–39 kg: 20 mg daily; ≥40 kg: 40 mg daily
dur: Usually up to 8 weeks for healing; ongoing for maintenance/hypersecretory states.
ix: Rilpivirine — contraindicated
High-dose methotrexate — ↑levels/toxicity
Acid-dependent drugs (ketoconazole, atazanavir, iron) — ↓absorption
Warfarin — possible ↑INR
Clopidogrel — preferred PPI (no important interaction, unlike omeprazole)
preg: No clear fetal-harm signal; acceptable when needed. Minimal milk transfer — generally compatible with breastfeeding.

dA: Highly emetogenic chemo: 24 mg PO once, 30 min before (or 0.15 mg/kg IV, max 16 mg/dose)
Moderately emetogenic chemo: 8 mg PO BID
Post-op: 4 mg IV/IM at induction, or 16 mg PO 1 h before anesthesia
Radiation: 8 mg PO TID
dP: Chemo, 4–11 yr: 4 mg PO TID
Chemo IV (6 mo–18 yr): 0.15 mg/kg (max 16 mg) at 0, 4, 8 h
Gastroenteritis (off-label): weight-based ODT (2 mg 8–15 kg; 4 mg 15–30 kg; 8 mg >30 kg)
dur: As needed around chemo, radiation, or surgery — a single dose to a few days.
ix: Apomorphine — contraindicated (profound hypotension, LOC)
QT-prolonging drugs (antiarrhythmics, antipsychotics, methadone) — additive torsades
Serotonergic drugs (SSRIs, SNRIs, fentanyl) — serotonin syndrome

Calcium channel blockers — additive AV block/hypotension

dA: Oral HTN: 10 mg PO QID x2-4 days, then 25 mg QID, up to 50 mg QID; usual 100-200 mg/day.

Beta-blockers — used together to blunt reflex tachycardia
NSAIDs — reduced antihypertensive effect

Severe cancer pain via epidural route

Tricyclic antidepressants — may blunt antihypertensive effect

Other laxatives — obscure the loose-stool titration endpoint
Antidiarrheals — reduce efficacy

Loop/thiazide diuretics — additive hypokalemia

dA: 875 mg/125 mg PO BID (every 12 hours) for most infections

2000 mg/125 mg ER PO BID for CAP or resistant sinusitis

Methotrexate — decreased clearance/increased toxicity

dA: 500 mg PO q6h (or q12h for mild infections) for cellulitis/UTI

Warfarin — possible enhanced anticoagulation
Nephrotoxic agents — increased renal toxicity risk

uses: Empiric therapy for sepsis and serious gram-negative infections incl. Pseudomonas

Reserve for patients with no alternative for uncomplicated infections.

Corticosteroids — increased tendon rupture risk
preg: No adequate controlled studies; use only if benefit justifies risk. Excreted in breast milk; short courses may be compatible with monitoring.

Fluoroquinolones — possible antagonism
Live typhoid vaccine — reduced efficacy

boxed: Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhea and colitis, which may be fatal, has been reported with nearly all antibacterials including clindamycin; reserve for serious infections where less toxic alternatives are inappropriate.

Limit total acetaminophen to <4,000 mg/day from all sources

Other acetaminophen products — additive hepatotoxicity
Serotonergic drugs — serotonin syndrome risk

ix: Benzodiazepines/alcohol/CNS depressants — profound sedation and respiratory depression
MAO inhibitors — potentiation; avoid within 14 days
Serotonergic drugs — serotonin syndrome risk

Anticholinergics — urinary retention and ileus

CYP3A4 inhibitors (azoles, macrolides, protease inhibitors) — increased levels

uses: Relief of muscle spasm from acute musculoskeletal conditions
Adjunct to rest and physical therapy for muscle strain
Short-term relief of low back and neck spasm

May increase to 10 mg three times a day based on response
Do not use for longer than 2 to 3 weeks
Extended-release (Amrix): 15 to 30 mg once daily

ix: MAO inhibitors — hyperpyretic crisis and seizures; avoid within 14 days
Serotonergic drugs (SSRIs, SNRIs, tramadol) — serotonin syndrome risk
CNS depressants/alcohol — additive sedation
Anticholinergic agents — additive dry mouth, retention, confusion
Tricyclic antidepressants — additive anticholinergic and cardiac effects

uses: Spasticity from multiple sclerosis (flexor spasms, pain, clonus)

ix: CNS depressants/alcohol/opioids — additive sedation and respiratory depression
Benzodiazepines — enhanced CNS depression
Tricyclic antidepressants — additive muscle weakness/hypotension
Antihypertensives — additive hypotension

uses: Chronic gout and hyperuricemia (prevention of flares and tophi)
Prevention of tumor lysis / chemotherapy-induced hyperuricemia
Recurrent calcium oxalate/uric acid kidney stones

Maintenance 200-300 mg/day (mild), 400-600 mg/day (moderate-severe); max 800 mg/day
Consider HLA-B*5801 screening in high-risk ancestry before starting
dP: Used for hyperuricemia in pediatric malignancy; not routinely used in children for gout.
dur: Lifelong for chronic gout
se: Severe cutaneous reactions — SJS/TEN, DRESS (assoc. HLA-B*5801)
Acute gout flare on initiation (co-prescribe prophylaxis)
ix: Azathioprine / 6-mercaptopurine — blocked metabolism, severe myelosuppression (reduce dose 66-75%)
Ampicillin/amoxicillin — increased rash incidence
Thiazide/loop diuretics — increased hypersensitivity risk
Warfarin — enhanced anticoagulant effect
preg: Limited human data; crosses placenta — use only if benefit outweighs risk. In breast milk; use caution during lactation.

uses: Gout flare prophylaxis (esp. when starting urate-lowering therapy)
dA: Acute gout: 1.2 mg at first sign of flare, then 0.6 mg one hour later (max 1.8 mg/day)
Prophylaxis: 0.6 mg once or twice daily (max 1.2 mg/day)
Pericarditis: 0.5 mg twice daily (0.5 mg once daily if <70 kg) for 3 months acute, >=6 months recurrent
Reduce dose with renal/hepatic impairment or CYP3A4/P-gp inhibitors
dP: Familial Mediterranean Fever in children >=4 years; not routinely used for gout in children.
dur: Short course for acute flare; months for prophylaxis/pericarditis
se: Neuromuscular toxicity, myopathy, rhabdomyolysis (esp. renal impairment)
ix: Strong CYP3A4/P-gp inhibitors (clarithromycin, ketoconazole, cyclosporine) — fatal toxicity; contraindicated in renal/hepatic impairment
Statins/fibrates — increased myopathy and rhabdomyolysis risk
Grapefruit juice — raised colchicine levels
P-gp inhibitors (verapamil, diltiazem) — increased exposure
preg: Human data have not shown a clear increased risk of major defects; use if clearly needed. Small amounts in breast milk; generally compatible with monitoring.

boxed: DOSED ONCE WEEKLY for RA/psoriasis — accidental daily dosing is fatal; use only by experienced clinicians.
Embryo-fetal toxicity — contraindicated in pregnancy for non-neoplastic disease (abortifacient, teratogen).
Hepatotoxicity — fibrosis and cirrhosis with chronic use.
Myelosuppression — severe bone marrow suppression, aplastic anemia.
Pulmonary toxicity — acute or chronic interstitial pneumonitis.
Serious infections, renal toxicity, severe GI toxicity, and secondary malignancies.
dA: RA: 7.5 mg ONCE WEEKLY orally; titrate to usual 10-25 mg once weekly (NOT daily)
Give folic acid (1 mg/day) or folinic acid to reduce toxicity
May split weekly oral dose or switch to SC injection if GI intolerance
Monitor CBC, LFTs, and renal function regularly
dP: Used once weekly for JIA and pediatric malignancy under specialist care; weight-based dosing.
dur: Chronic, ongoing weekly therapy
ix: NSAIDs — reduced clearance, severe/fatal hematologic and GI toxicity (esp. high dose)
Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole — additive antifolate effect, marrow suppression (avoid)
Proton pump inhibitors — reduced elimination, increased levels
Penicillins/probenecid — decreased renal clearance, raised levels
preg: Contraindicated in pregnancy for non-cancer indications — abortifacient and teratogenic. Effective contraception required (stop >=1 ovulatory cycle before conception). Contraindicated during breastfeeding.

dA: RA: 400-600 mg/day initially, maintenance 200-400 mg/day
Lupus: 200-400 mg/day
Do NOT exceed 5 mg/kg/day (actual body weight) to limit retinopathy risk
Baseline and annual ophthalmologic exams (retinopathy screening)
dP: Used for JIA and pediatric lupus; weight-based dosing (<=5 mg/kg/day).
dur: Chronic, long-term (effect on RA/lupus takes weeks-months)
se: Myelosuppression; severe skin reactions; skin hyperpigmentation
ix: QT-prolonging drugs (azithromycin, antiarrhythmics) — additive arrhythmia risk
Digoxin — increased levels
Insulin/antidiabetics — enhanced hypoglycemia
Tamoxifen — increased retinal toxicity risk
preg: Extensive data show no clear increased defect risk; often continued in pregnancy for lupus as benefits outweigh risks. Small amounts in breast milk; considered compatible.

boxed: Serious infections: increased risk of serious, sometimes fatal infections including tuberculosis (reactivation), invasive fungal infections, and sepsis.
Malignancy: lymphoma (including hepatosplenic T-cell lymphoma) and other malignancies, some fatal, reported in children and adolescents.
dA: RA/PsA/AS: 40 mg SC every other week
Crohn's/UC: 160 mg on day 1, 80 mg on day 15, then 40 mg every other week from day 29
Plaque psoriasis: 80 mg initial, then 40 mg every other week starting one week later
Screen for latent TB and hepatitis B before starting
dP: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis (>=2 yr): weight-based, 10-40 mg SC every other week.
dur: Chronic; long-term with periodic reassessment of response and infection risk
se: Upper respiratory and other serious infections
Reactivation of latent TB or hepatitis B
Increased risk of lymphoma and other malignancies
Rare demyelinating disease and drug-induced lupus
ix: Live vaccines — avoid during immunosuppression
Anakinra or abatacept — increased serious infection risk; avoid combination
Other biologic DMARDs/TNF blockers — additive immunosuppression
Rituximab — heightened infection risk
Warfarin/theophylline/cyclosporine — cytokine normalization may alter levels
preg: Crosses the placenta (esp. third trimester) and may affect neonatal immune response — delay live vaccines in exposed infants. Minimal amounts in breast milk; generally compatible.

dA: Osteoporosis treatment: 70 mg PO once weekly or 10 mg PO once daily
Osteoporosis prevention: 35 mg once weekly or 5 mg once daily
Paget disease: 40 mg once daily for 6 months
Take on arising with a full glass of plain water, >=30 min before food/drink/other meds; remain upright >=30 min
dP: Not routinely used in children.
dur: Long-term; reassess need after 3-5 years (atypical fracture risk)
hl: Terminal half-life exceeding 10 years (slow release from bone)
ix: Calcium supplements — reduce absorption; separate dosing
Antacids and multivalent cations (Ca, Mg, Al, Fe) — impair absorption; give >=30 min apart
NSAIDs — additive upper GI irritation
Aspirin — increased upper GI adverse effects
preg: Crosses the placenta and may affect fetal skeletal development; generally avoided in pregnancy. Unknown whether excreted in breast milk.

uses: Prevention of hypokalemia in at-risk patients (e.g., diuretic use)
Metabolic alkalosis associated with potassium depletion
dA: Oral treatment: 40-100 mEq/day in 2-5 divided doses; single dose typically <=20 mEq
Oral prevention: about 20 mEq/day, titrated to serum potassium
IV (non-urgent): infuse at <=10 mEq/hour, concentration <=40 mEq/L peripherally
IV (urgent, K <2 with ECG changes): up to 40 mEq/hour with continuous cardiac monitoring, central line
Never give IV potassium undiluted
dP: Hypokalemia: 2-4 mEq/kg/day PO divided; single dose <=1 mEq/kg or 40 mEq, up to 100 mEq/day.
dur: Short-term for acute correction or ongoing for chronic loss, guided by serum monitoring
se: GI ulceration/bleeding with solid oral forms
Pain and phlebitis at IV site
Peaked T waves and ECG changes with excess
ix: ACE inhibitors — reduced potassium excretion causing hyperkalemia
ARBs — additive hyperkalemia
Potassium-sparing diuretics (spironolactone, amiloride) — hyperkalemia
Anticholinergics — delayed GI transit increases mucosal ulceration risk
NSAIDs — impaired renal potassium handling
preg: Replacement to maintain normal serum levels is compatible with pregnancy; potassium is a normal milk constituent, so lactation use is acceptable.

pills.s: IV concentrate (2 mEq/mL), must be diluted

uses: Prevention and treatment of seizures in preeclampsia/eclampsia

Monitor reflexes, respiratory rate, urine output; keep IV calcium gluconate available as antidote

Calcium channel blockers (nifedipine) — additive hypotension and weakness
CNS depressants — additive sedation and respiratory depression
Aminoglycosides — additive neuromuscular blockade

pills.s: 50% injection (500 mg/mL); dilute before IV use

uses: Calcium channel blocker and magnesium toxicity
Adjunct in cardiac arrest with documented hypocalcemia/hyperkalemia
dA: Hyperkalemia (cardiac stabilization): 1-2 g (10-20 mL of 10%) IV over 2-5 min with ECG monitoring; may repeat
Symptomatic hypocalcemia: 1-2 g IV slowly, repeated per response
Prefer central or large peripheral vein; infuse slowly to avoid arrhythmia
Watch for extravasation — can cause severe tissue necrosis
dP: Hypocalcemia: 29-60 mg/kg (~0.3-0.6 mL/kg of 10%) IV slowly; not through scalp veins.
dur: Acute/short-term for emergent correction; repeat guided by ionized calcium
se: Bradycardia and arrhythmias with rapid IV push

Ceftriaxone — forms insoluble precipitates; do not co-administer (esp. neonates)
Thiazide diuretics — reduced calcium excretion, hypercalcemia
Calcium channel blockers — calcium antagonizes their effect
preg: Used to correct maternal hypocalcemia and generally acceptable when clinically indicated. Calcium is a normal milk component; compatible with breastfeeding.

uses: Adjunct in hyperkalemia to shift potassium intracellularly
Cardiotoxicity from TCA (or other sodium-channel-blocker) overdose
Urinary alkalinization to enhance elimination of weak acids (e.g., salicylates)

Urinary alkalinization: titrate infusion to urine pH >7.5

hl: Physiologic buffer regulated by kidneys and lungs (no discrete half-life)
se: Hypokalemia and ionized hypocalcemia with alkalosis

Calcium-containing solutions — precipitation; do not co-administer in same line
Corticosteroids — additive sodium/fluid retention
Urinary alkalinization — increases clearance of weak acids (salicylates, lithium) and decreases clearance of weak bases (amphetamines)
Enteric-coated/delayed-release drugs — raised gastric pH alters release
preg: No evidence of fetal harm; acceptable when clearly needed for maternal acid-base correction. Compatible with breastfeeding.

uses: Prevention/treatment of iron deficiency (pregnancy, chronic blood loss, dietary shortfall)
Iron repletion in menstruating or bariatric patients

Take on empty stomach (or with food if GI upset); vitamin C may enhance absorption
Continue 3-6 months after hemoglobin normalizes to replenish stores

dur: Continue 3-6 months after hemoglobin corrects to rebuild stores
hl: No fixed plasma half-life (iron physiologically retained)
se: GI upset: nausea, epigastric pain, constipation, diarrhea
Acute overdose (esp. children) causes serious/fatal toxicity
ix: Tetracyclines and fluoroquinolones — chelation reduces absorption of both; separate by 2-4 h

PPIs / H2 blockers / antacids — reduced iron absorption

uses: Treatment of megaloblastic/macrocytic anemia due to folate deficiency

Adjunct to reduce toxicity of some antifolate drugs (e.g., low-dose methotrexate)

dP: Deficiency: infants 0.1 mg/day, children 0.3-1 mg/day PO, titrated to response.
dur: Deficiency: until hematologic recovery, then maintenance; prevention through first trimester
hl: Rapidly metabolized to active folate coenzymes; stored in liver
se: May mask hematologic signs of B12 deficiency while neurologic damage progresses
High doses: altered sleep, irritability, GI upset (uncommon)
ix: Vitamin B12 deficiency — corrects anemia but masks B12 deficiency; rule out B12 deficiency first
Phenytoin — folate may lower phenytoin levels; phenytoin also lowers folate
Methotrexate — antifolate action antagonized (relevant in non-cancer dosing)
Sulfasalazine — impairs folate absorption
Trimethoprim/pyrimethamine — reduce folate activation
preg: Recommended in pregnancy; reduces neural tube defect risk (Category A at recommended doses). In breast milk; compatible with breastfeeding.

uses: Treatment of vitamin B12 deficiency and pernicious anemia
Correction of megaloblastic anemia from B12 deficiency
B12 repletion in malabsorption, gastrectomy, ileal disease, or vegan diet
dA: Pernicious anemia: 1000 mcg IM or deep SC once daily for 6-7 days, then taper to every-other-day and less frequent
Maintenance: 100-1000 mcg IM/deep SC once monthly for life
High-dose oral alternative: 1000-2000 mcg PO daily (effective even in pernicious anemia)
Intranasal spray (500 mcg) once weekly available for maintenance
dP: B12 deficiency: 0.2-1 mg IM/deep SC individualized to severity; maintenance thereafter.
dur: Lifelong for pernicious anemia / irreversible malabsorption
hl: Serum ~6 days, but large hepatic stores (body stores last months-years)
se: Hypokalemia early in treatment of severe megaloblastic anemia
ix: Metformin — long-term use reduces B12 absorption/levels
PPIs and H2 blockers — reduce B12 absorption from food
Chloramphenicol — may blunt hematologic response
Colchicine — may decrease B12 absorption
Folic acid — high doses can mask B12 deficiency
preg: Recommended dietary amounts are safe and needed in pregnancy; deficiency should be treated. Compatible with breastfeeding.

uses: Prevention and treatment of vitamin D deficiency
Adjunct with calcium for osteoporosis prevention and treatment
Support of bone mineralization; prevention of rickets/osteomalacia
Supplementation in malabsorption, limited sun exposure, or older adults
dA: Maintenance/prevention: 800-2000 IU PO daily (RDA 600 IU <=70 yr, 800 IU >70)
Deficiency repletion: 50,000 IU PO once weekly for 6-8 weeks, then maintenance
Osteoporosis: 800-2000 IU daily with adequate calcium
Tolerable upper intake ~4000 IU/day for most adults
dP: Deficiency/rickets prevention: infants 400 IU/day; children 600 IU/day, higher for documented deficiency under monitoring.
dur: Deficiency: weekly high-dose 6-8 weeks then maintenance; prevention/osteoporosis: ongoing daily
hl: Cholecalciferol ~1 day; circulating 25-OH vitamin D ~2-3 weeks
se: Excess causes hypercalcemia: nausea, vomiting, constipation, weakness
Confusion, arrhythmias in severe hypervitaminosis D
ix: Thiazide diuretics — reduced calcium excretion, hypercalcemia risk
Digoxin — vitamin-D-induced hypercalcemia potentiates digoxin toxicity
Cholestyramine/orlistat/mineral oil — reduced vitamin D absorption
Corticosteroids — antagonize vitamin D effect on calcium absorption
Phenytoin/phenobarbital — accelerate vitamin D metabolism
preg: Recommended intakes are safe and needed; correct deficiency but avoid excessive doses (fetal hypercalcemia). Compatible with breastfeeding.

uses: Treatment and prevention of thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency
Wernicke encephalopathy in alcohol use disorder or malnutrition
Empiric repletion in altered mental status or alcohol withdrawal
dA: Wernicke encephalopathy: 100-500 mg IV (typically 200-500 mg) three times daily until symptoms resolve
Suspected deficiency/alcohol use: 100 mg IV or IM; give BEFORE glucose to avoid precipitating Wernicke
Maintenance after acute repletion: 50-100 mg IM/IV daily until oral intake adequate
General deficiency: 5-100 mg IV/IM three times daily, or 5-30 mg PO daily
dP: Infantile beriberi: 10-25 mg IM/IV daily; dietary deficiency 10-50 mg PO daily divided.
dur: Continue until clinical deficiency resolves and dietary intake resumes
hl: Water-soluble with rapid renal clearance once tissue stores saturated
ix: IV dextrose/glucose — giving glucose before thiamine can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy
Neuromuscular blocking agents — thiamine may enhance effect
Loop diuretics — chronic use increases thiamine losses
Assay interference — may alter theophylline, uric acid, urobilinogen tests
preg: A normal dietary requirement and considered safe in pregnancy (Category A). In breast milk; caution with high parenteral doses.

uses: Reversal of benzodiazepine-induced sedation after anesthesia or procedural sedation

Diagnostic aid to confirm benzodiazepine contribution to CNS depression
dA: Reversal of sedation: 0.2 mg IV over 15 sec; if inadequate, repeat 0.2 mg at 1-min intervals to max total 1 mg (usual 0.6-1 mg)
Suspected overdose: 0.2 mg IV over 30 sec, then 0.3 mg, then 0.5 mg at 1-min intervals to max total 3 mg
Resedation: repeat at 20-min intervals, no more than 1 mg per dose and 3 mg per hour
dP: Reversal of sedation (age >=1 yr): 0.01 mg/kg (max 0.2 mg) IV over 15 sec; repeat 0.01 mg/kg at 1-min intervals to max cumulative 0.05 mg/kg or 1 mg.
dur: Single procedural use; short half-life means monitor for resedation and re-dose
se: Seizures, especially in benzodiazepine-dependent or mixed overdose
ix: Chronic benzodiazepines — reversal can precipitate acute withdrawal and seizures
TCA/cyclic antidepressant overdose — unmasks proconvulsant effects; high seizure risk
Benzodiazepines controlling status epilepticus/ICP — reversal removes seizure protection
Non-benzodiazepine sedatives (barbiturates, opioids, alcohol) — flumazenil does NOT reverse them
preg: Use only if benefit justifies risk; not recommended during labor and delivery. Milk excretion unknown; use caution.

uses: Antidote for acetaminophen overdose to prevent hepatotoxicity
Mucolytic for viscid secretions in bronchopulmonary disease
Adjunct in acute liver failure of various causes
dA: IV 21-hour protocol: 150 mg/kg over 1 hour, then 50 mg/kg over 4 hours, then 100 mg/kg over 16 hours
Oral protocol: 140 mg/kg loading dose, then 70 mg/kg every 4 hours for 17 doses
Start based on serum acetaminophen level on the Rumack-Matthew nomogram; give within 8 hours of ingestion for maximal benefit
dP: Same weight-based IV and oral regimens as adults; dilute IV doses in smaller fluid volumes for children <40 kg.
dur: Complete the 21-hour IV or ~72-hour oral course; extend if liver injury or detectable acetaminophen
hl: ~5.6 h IV, ~6.25 h oral (longer in hepatic impairment)
se: Anaphylactoid reactions (flushing, rash, angioedema) esp. during IV loading
ix: Activated charcoal — may reduce absorption of oral acetylcysteine
Nitroglycerin — additive hypotension and headache
Some antibiotics — physically incompatible; do not mix in nebulizer
Rubber/metals (iron, copper) — react with mucolytic solution; avoid contact
preg: Crosses the placenta and is the treatment of choice for acetaminophen overdose in pregnancy; benefit outweighs risk. With IV therapy, consider discarding milk ~30 hours after dosing.

uses: Medical expulsive therapy for distal ureteral stones (off-label)
dA: 0.4 mg PO once daily, taken 30 minutes after the same meal each day
May increase to 0.8 mg once daily after 2-4 weeks if response inadequate
Swallow capsule whole; do not crush, chew, or open
If a dose lapses for several days, restart at 0.4 mg
dP: Not routinely used in children.
dur: Chronic ongoing therapy for BPH; short courses (<=4 weeks) for stone expulsion
ix: PDE5 inhibitors (sildenafil, tadalafil) — additive hypotension
Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole) — raise levels, hypotension
Strong CYP2D6 inhibitors (paroxetine) and cimetidine — increased exposure
Other alpha-blockers / antihypertensives — additive BP lowering

Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole, ritonavir) — increased exposure

Do not use to prevent cardiovascular disease or dementia; use lowest effective dose for shortest duration.

Smoking — increased thromboembolic/cardiovascular risk

boxed: Indicated only for medical induction of labor, not elective induction (labor initiated for convenience without a medical indication).

Hypotension and reflex tachycardia with rapid IV push

Cyclopropane anesthesia — hypotension and arrhythmias
Prostaglandins — potentiated uterotonic effect, risk of tachysystole
Regional anesthetics — additive cardiovascular effects

boxed: Severe, sometimes fatal hypersensitivity reactions including anaphylaxis have occurred during and immediately after IV (and IM) injection; restrict IV/IM use to when other routes are not feasible and administer IV slowly.

Hypoprothrombinemia from malabsorption or drug-induced deficiency

Higher doses (up to 25-50 mg) for severe deficiency/bleeding
Repeat based on INR response (INR often improves in 12-14 hours)

se: Transient warfarin resistance after high doses
ix: Warfarin/coumarin anticoagulants — antagonizes effect, may cause temporary warfarin resistance
Bile acid sequestrants (cholestyramine) — reduced vitamin K absorption
Orlistat — decreased absorption
Broad-spectrum antibiotics — may potentiate deficiency

boxed: Serious, sometimes fatal events in the risk-reduction setting: uterine malignancies (endometrial adenocarcinoma and uterine sarcoma), stroke, and pulmonary embolism.

Reduction of breast cancer incidence in high-risk women
Ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) after surgery/radiation

Doses of 20-40 mg/day for metastatic disease; give doses above 20 mg in divided doses

ix: Strong CYP2D6 inhibitors (paroxetine, fluoxetine) — reduce active metabolite, may lower efficacy

Rifampin (CYP3A4 inducer) — markedly reduced tamoxifen levels

uses: Inflammation and itching in corticosteroid-responsive dermatoses

Discontinue when control is achieved; avoid prolonged high-potency use

dur: Short-term; reassess if no improvement in ~2 weeks
hl: Minimal systemic absorption through intact skin
se: Burning, itching, or stinging at application site
ix: Other topical products on same site — altered absorption/irritation
Concurrent systemic corticosteroids — additive systemic effects with extensive use
Occlusive dressings — increased absorption and adverse effects

uses: Impetigo and secondary skin infections due to S. aureus and S. pyogenes

Systemic drug interactions — clinically insignificant (minimal absorption)
Polyethylene glycol vehicle — caution with large open wounds and renal impairment
Chloramphenicol — potential antagonism

uses: Relief of sneezing, rhinorrhea, nasal/ocular pruritus, watery eyes

Alcohol — additive sedation and impairment

Theophylline — decreased cetirizine clearance at higher doses

Alcohol — additive CNS depression
Other anticholinergics — additive anticholinergic toxicity
MAO inhibitors — intensified and prolonged anticholinergic effects

Titrate to lowest effective dose

uses: Adjunct to standard HF therapy in self-identified Black patients to improve survival
Prolong time to heart failure hospitalization

Alcohol — potentiates hypotension

Added when other antianginals inadequately control symptoms

Titrate to 1000 mg twice daily (max 1000 mg BID)

QT-prolonging drugs — additive QT prolongation

Simvastatin — increased exposure; limit to 20 mg/day

boxed: To minimize the risk of induced arrhythmia (torsades/QT prolongation), initiate and reinitiate sotalol in a facility that can provide cardiac resuscitation, continuous ECG monitoring, and creatinine clearance calculation. Do not substitute Betapace for Betapace AF.

ix: Warfarin — reduced absorption/anticoagulant effect
Digoxin — reduced absorption
Levothyroxine — reduced absorption
Many oral drugs — bind resin; give >=1 h before or 4-6 h after cholestyramine
preg: Not systemically absorbed but may impair maternal fat-soluble vitamin/folate absorption; supplement as needed. Considered compatible with breastfeeding.

boxed: Contraindicated in patients with heart failure of any severity; phosphodiesterase-3 inhibitors have decreased survival in patients with heart failure.
uses: Reduce claudication symptoms and improve walking distance in peripheral arterial disease
dA: 100 mg orally twice daily, >=30 min before or 2 h after breakfast and dinner
Reduce to 50 mg twice daily with strong CYP3A4 or CYP2C19 inhibitors
Symptom benefit may take up to 12 weeks
dP: Not routinely used in children.
dur: Chronic; assess benefit after ~3 months.
ix: Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole, clarithromycin) — increased levels; reduce dose
Strong CYP2C19 inhibitors (omeprazole, fluvoxamine) — increased levels; reduce dose
Other antiplatelets/anticoagulants — increased bleeding risk
Grapefruit juice — raises cilostazol concentration
preg: Animal data show adverse effects; not recommended unless clearly needed. Discontinue drug or nursing due to potential infant risk.

boxed: Premature discontinuation increases the risk of thrombotic events; if stopped for a reason other than pathological bleeding or treatment completion, consider covering with another anticoagulant.
Spinal/epidural hematoma may occur with neuraxial anesthesia or spinal puncture, which can cause long-term or permanent paralysis.
uses: Reduce stroke/systemic embolism risk in non-valvular atrial fibrillation
Treatment of DVT and PE after 5-10 days of parenteral anticoagulation
dA: Atrial fibrillation: 150 mg twice daily (CrCl >30 mL/min)

Hip replacement prophylaxis: 110 mg 1-4 h post-op, then 220 mg once daily for 28-35 days
Renal (CrCl 15-30 in AFib): 75 mg twice daily
dP: Ages 8+ (VTE), weight-based capsules (e.g., 41 to <61 kg = 185 mg BID; >=81 kg = 260 mg BID)
dur: Twice-daily dosing.
ix: P-gp inhibitors (ketoconazole, dronedarone, verapamil) — increased levels and bleeding
P-gp inducers (rifampin) — reduced levels; avoid
Antiplatelets/other anticoagulants — additive bleeding
NSAIDs — increased GI/bleeding risk
SSRIs/SNRIs — increased bleeding
preg: May increase maternal and fetal bleeding, particularly at delivery; use only if benefit justifies risk. Breastfeeding not recommended (data lacking).

boxed: Can cause significant, sometimes fatal bleeding. Do not use with active pathological bleeding or a history of TIA or stroke. Generally not recommended in patients >=75 years. Do not start in patients likely to undergo urgent CABG; discontinue >=7 days before surgery. Additional risk with body weight <60 kg. Do not discontinue prematurely (thrombotic risk).
uses: Reduce thrombotic CV events (incl. stent thrombosis) in ACS managed with PCI
Unstable angina or NSTEMI undergoing PCI
STEMI managed with primary or delayed PCI
dA: Loading dose: 60 mg once
Maintenance: 10 mg once daily
Consider 5 mg once daily if <60 kg
Give with daily aspirin 75-325 mg
dP: Not routinely used in children.
dur: Once daily; irreversible platelet inhibition (~7-10 days).
ix: Anticoagulants (warfarin, heparin, DOACs) — additive bleeding
NSAIDs (chronic) — increased bleeding
Other antiplatelets — additive bleeding
SSRIs/SNRIs — increased bleeding
Opioids — delayed/reduced absorption of oral P2Y12 inhibitors
preg: No adequate data; use only if clearly needed with awareness of delivery bleeding risk. Milk transfer unknown.

uses: Reversal of dabigatran anticoagulation for emergency surgery/urgent procedures
Reversal of dabigatran in life-threatening or uncontrolled bleeding
dA: 5 g IV, given as two consecutive 2.5 g/50 mL vials as bolus injections or rapid infusion
A second 5 g dose may be considered if clinically relevant bleeding recurs with prolonged clotting times
dP: Not routinely used in children (safety and efficacy not established).
dur: Rapid, essentially immediate reversal.
se: Thromboembolic events (from underlying condition once reversed)
ix: No formal drug interaction studies; binds only dabigatran and does not reverse other anticoagulants
May be co-administered with standard supportive measures
preg: Limited systemic exposure; use only if clinical benefit outweighs risk. Milk excretion unknown.

uses: Neutralization of heparin during/after cardiac and vascular surgery
Reversal of heparin in dialysis/extracorporeal circuits
dA: 1 mg IV neutralizes ~100 USP units of heparin sodium
Reduce dose based on time since heparin (~half if 30-60 min elapsed)
Maximum single dose 50 mg, given slowly over ~10 min
Administer by slow IV injection to limit hypotension/anaphylactoid reactions
dP: Not routinely used in children (dosing individualized to heparin to be neutralized).
dur: Rapid onset (~5 min); heparin rebound bleeding may occur hours later.
ix: Heparin — neutralizes anticoagulant activity (intended effect)
Low-molecular-weight heparins — only partial neutralization
Protamine-containing insulins (NPH) — prior exposure increases hypersensitivity risk
Beta-blockers — may worsen hypotension
preg: No adequate studies; use only if clearly needed. Milk excretion unknown; caution in nursing mothers.

uses: Adjunct to diet/exercise for glycemic control in type 2 diabetes
Combination with metformin or insulin when single-agent therapy is inadequate
dA: Initial: 1-2 mg once daily with breakfast or the first main meal
Titrate in 1-2 mg increments no more often than every 1-2 weeks
Usual maintenance 1-4 mg once daily; maximum 8 mg once daily
Start 1 mg daily in elderly, debilitated, or renal impairment
dP: Not routinely used in children (weight gain and hypoglycemia risk).
dur: ~24 h (once daily).
ix: CYP2C9 inhibitors (fluconazole, gemfibrozil) — increased levels and hypoglycemia
Other sulfonamides, salicylates, protein-bound drugs — potentiate hypoglycemia
Beta-blockers — mask hypoglycemia and impair recovery
Colesevelam — reduces absorption; give glimepiride >=4 h before
Thiazides, corticosteroids — reduce glycemic control
preg: Not recommended in pregnancy; insulin is preferred, and discontinue >=2 weeks before delivery to avoid neonatal hypoglycemia. Breastfeeding not recommended (infant hypoglycemia risk).

uses: Adjunct to diet/exercise for glycemic control in type 2 diabetes
Historically used off-label for gestational diabetes (now less favored)
dA: Standard tablets: start 2.5-5 mg once daily with breakfast
Titrate by 2.5 mg/day weekly; maintenance 1.25-20 mg/day; max 20 mg/day
Micronized (Glynase): start 1.5-3 mg once daily; max 12 mg/day
Elderly/renal/hepatic: start 1.25 mg (standard) or 0.75 mg (micronized) daily
dP: Not routinely used in children; safety and efficacy not established under 18 years.
dur: Hypoglycemic action ~24 h; once or twice daily.
se: Hypoglycemia (can be prolonged/severe in elderly or renal impairment)
ix: Alcohol — disulfiram-like reaction and enhanced hypoglycemia
CYP2C9 inhibitors (fluconazole) — increased levels and hypoglycemia
Beta-blockers — mask hypoglycemia and impair recovery
Other sulfonamides/antibiotics — potentiate hypoglycemia
Bosentan — contraindicated (hepatotoxicity risk)
preg: Crosses the placenta minimally and has been used for GDM, but insulin is generally preferred; use near term may cause neonatal hypoglycemia. Monitor breastfed infants for hypoglycemia.

boxed: Thyroid C-cell tumors (including medullary thyroid carcinoma) in rodents. Contraindicated in patients with a personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma or MEN 2.
uses: Adjunct to diet/exercise for glycemic control in type 2 diabetes (Victoza)
Reduce MACE in type 2 diabetes with established CV disease (Victoza)
Chronic weight management in obesity/overweight, adults and adolescents >=12 yr (Saxenda)
dA: Victoza: 0.6 mg SC daily x1 week, then 1.2 mg daily; may increase to 1.8 mg; max 1.8 mg/day
Saxenda: weekly titration 0.6 -> 1.2 -> 1.8 -> 2.4 -> 3 mg once daily; max 3 mg/day
Inject SC (abdomen, thigh, upper arm) at any time of day, independent of meals
dP: Victoza (>=10 yr, T2DM): start 0.6 mg SC daily, titrate to 1.2-1.8 mg; Saxenda (>=12 yr, >=60 kg): follow adult titration
dur: Once-daily dosing.
se: Increased heart rate; acute kidney injury from volume depletion
ix: Insulin or sulfonylureas — additive hypoglycemia; reduce their dose
Oral drugs — delayed gastric emptying can alter absorption
Other GLP-1 agonists or DPP-4 inhibitors — do not co-administer
Warfarin/narrow-index oral drugs — monitor due to altered absorption
preg: Not recommended; discontinue when pregnancy is recognized (Saxenda contraindicated). Milk excretion unknown; weigh benefits against risk.

uses: Adjunct to diet/exercise for glycemic control in type 2 diabetes
Reduce MACE in type 2 diabetes with established CV disease
Reduce risk of end-stage kidney disease and CV death in diabetic kidney disease with albuminuria
dA: Start 100 mg once daily before the first meal
May increase to max 300 mg once daily if eGFR >=60 and additional control needed
eGFR 30 to <60: limit to 100 mg once daily
Withhold >=3 days before major surgery or prolonged fasting (ketoacidosis risk)
dP: Type 2 diabetes (>=10 yr): start 100 mg once daily before the first meal; may increase to 300 mg
dur: Once daily.
ix: UGT inducers (rifampin, phenytoin, ritonavir) — reduce exposure; consider dose increase
Diuretics — additive volume depletion and hypotension
Insulin/sulfonylureas — increased hypoglycemia
Digoxin — increased digoxin levels; monitor
preg: Not recommended in the 2nd/3rd trimesters (fetal renal development). Breastfeeding not recommended (developing kidney).

uses: Glycemic control in type 1 diabetes (>=1 yr)
Glycemic control in type 2 diabetes (>=1 yr)
dA: Insulin-naive T1DM: ~1/3 to 1/2 of total daily insulin as basal, remainder as mealtime rapid-acting
Insulin-naive T2DM: start 10 units once daily
Switching from another basal insulin: start at the same total daily units
Give once daily at any time; titrate no more often than every 3-4 days
dP: T1DM/T2DM (>=1 yr): once daily at the same time; when switching, start at 80% of prior dose
dur: Ultra-long, >42 h; steady state in 3-4 days.
ix: Sulfonylureas, GLP-1 agonists, other glucose-lowering drugs — additive hypoglycemia
Beta-blockers, clonidine — may mask hypoglycemia
Thiazolidinediones — fluid retention/heart failure when combined with insulin
Thiazides, corticosteroids, sympathomimetics — raise glucose
preg: Insulin is preferred in pregnancy with tight control. Considered compatible with breastfeeding.

uses: Intermediate-acting basal coverage, often twice daily
dA: Individualize; total daily insulin often ~0.2-0.4 units/kg/day initially
Commonly given twice daily (before breakfast and at bedtime/dinner)
Administer subcutaneously; do not give IV
Titrate to self-monitored glucose; may combine with mealtime insulin
dP: Used in pediatric type 1 diabetes; dose individualized by weight and glucose monitoring, usually twice daily
dur: Onset ~1-3 h, peak ~4-12 h, duration ~12-18 h; usually twice daily.
hl: Intermediate-acting; glucose-lowering effect up to ~18 h.
ix: Sulfonylureas, GLP-1 agonists — additive hypoglycemia
Beta-blockers, clonidine — mask hypoglycemia
Thiazolidinediones — fluid retention/heart failure with insulin
Corticosteroids, thiazides, sympathomimetics, atypical antipsychotics — raise glucose
preg: Insulin is standard of care in pregnancy; NPH has long clinical experience. Compatible with breastfeeding.

boxed: Severe hepatic injury and acute liver failure, some fatal or requiring transplant, reported in adults and children. Reserve for patients intolerant of methimazole and not candidates for surgery/radioactive iodine, or in first-trimester pregnancy.
uses: Hyperthyroidism (Graves disease) when methimazole is unsuitable
Thyroid storm (blocks synthesis and peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion)
Preferred first-trimester agent for hyperthyroidism in pregnancy
Preparation for thyroidectomy or radioactive iodine
dA: Hyperthyroidism: 300 mg/day in 3 divided doses (q8h); severe up to 400-900 mg/day
Maintenance: 100-150 mg/day divided
Thyroid storm: loading 500 mg-1 g, then 250 mg q4h
dP: Reserved for children intolerant of methimazole; initiate ~50 mg/day with close hepatic monitoring
dur: Three times daily; higher/more frequent in thyroid storm.
ix: Warfarin — altered anticoagulant effect; monitor INR
Beta-blockers — clearance rises as euthyroid restored
Digoxin — levels may rise with euthyroidism
Theophylline — reduced clearance; may need dose reduction
preg: Preferred antithyroid agent in the first trimester (methimazole carries higher teratogenic risk), then switch to methimazole given PTU hepatotoxicity. Minimally excreted in milk and considered compatible with breastfeeding at moderate doses.

uses: Mineralocorticoid replacement in primary adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
dA: Addison disease: 0.1 mg daily (range 0.1 mg 3x/week up to 0.2 mg daily), with hydrocortisone or cortisone
Reduce to 0.05 mg daily if transient hypertension develops
dP: Used in salt-losing CAH, typically 0.05-0.2 mg daily with a glucocorticoid; monitor growth, BP, and electrolytes
dur: Once daily.
se: Congestive heart failure with excess dose
Growth suppression in children with prolonged use
ix: Potassium-depleting diuretics — additive hypokalemia
Digoxin — hypokalemia potentiates digitalis toxicity
NSAIDs — increased sodium/fluid retention and GI risk
Phenytoin/rifampin/barbiturates — enhanced metabolism; may need higher dose
preg: Use only if benefit justifies risk, monitoring maternal edema and hypertension. Corticosteroids distribute into milk; use caution while nursing.

dA: Central DI oral: start 0.05 mg BID; usual 0.1-0.8 mg/day divided
Central DI intranasal: 10-40 mcg/day once or in 2-3 divided doses
Hemophilia A/vWD: 0.3 mcg/kg IV (max ~20 mcg) over 15-30 min; may repeat q8-12h
Monitor sodium and restrict fluids to avoid hyponatremia
dP: Central DI (>=4 yr) intranasal: start 10 mcg daily; oral start 0.05 mg BID
Hemophilia A/vWD (>=3 mo): 0.3 mcg/kg IV over 15-30 min with fluid restriction
dur: Once to 2-3 times daily (DI); as-needed for bleeding.
se: Hyponatremia — can be severe, causing seizures/coma/death (monitor sodium, restrict fluids)
ix: SSRIs/TCAs — increased hyponatremia risk
Carbamazepine/lamotrigine — increased hyponatremia risk
NSAIDs — increased hyponatremia risk
Loop diuretics and systemic glucocorticoids — increased hyponatremia risk
preg: Placental transfer is low and it is widely used in pregnant women with DI. Only negligible amounts appear in breast milk; regarded as compatible.

boxed: Severe hypocalcemia in patients with advanced CKD (eGFR <30), including dialysis patients, can be fatal (Prolia). Evaluate for CKD-MBD and monitor serum calcium before and during therapy.
uses: Postmenopausal osteoporosis at high fracture risk (Prolia)
Bone loss from androgen- or aromatase-inhibitor therapy (Prolia)
Prevention of skeletal-related events in bone metastases (Xgeva)
Giant cell tumor of bone; hypercalcemia of malignancy (Xgeva)
dA: Prolia: 60 mg SC every 6 months (with calcium and vitamin D)
Xgeva: 120 mg SC every 4 weeks
dP: Prolia not indicated in children. Xgeva: skeletally mature adolescents with giant cell tumor — 120 mg SC q4wk plus days 8 and 15 of the first month
dur: Prolia every 6 months; Xgeva every 4 weeks.
ix: Calcimimetics (cinacalcet) — additive hypocalcemia
Immunosuppressants — increased serious infection risk
Other calcium-lowering agents — additive hypocalcemia
Concurrent bone-modifying antibody — do not co-administer (Prolia/Xgeva same drug)
preg: Contraindicated in pregnancy (Prolia) and can cause fetal harm; use effective contraception during and for 5 months after the last dose. Breastfeeding not recommended.

uses: Hypocalcemia in dialysis-dependent chronic kidney disease
dA: Dialysis hypocalcemia (oral): start 0.25 mcg daily; usual 0.5-1 mcg daily
Predialysis secondary hyperparathyroidism: 0.25 mcg daily, up to 0.5 mcg daily
Hypoparathyroidism: 0.25 mcg daily; usual 0.5-2 mcg daily
IV (dialysis): 1-2 mcg 3x/week, range 0.5-4 mcg
dP: Dialysis hypocalcemia: 0.25-2 mcg daily
Predialysis <3 yr: 0.01-0.015 mcg/kg once daily; >=3 yr: 0.25 mcg, up to 0.5 mcg daily
dur: Once daily (oral); 3 times weekly (IV in dialysis).
ix: Thiazide diuretics — increased hypercalcemia risk
Digoxin — hypercalcemia may precipitate arrhythmias
Magnesium-containing antacids — hypermagnesemia in dialysis
Anticonvulsants (phenytoin/phenobarbital) — increased vitamin D catabolism
preg: Use only if potential benefit justifies risk, monitoring maternal calcium. Avoid nursing during therapy (risk of infant hypercalcemia).

boxed: Topical gels: secondary exposure via skin-to-skin contact can cause virilization in children and women; cover the application site and wash hands.
Class labeling: testosterone products can increase blood pressure, raising the risk of major adverse cardiovascular events.
uses: Replacement therapy for male hypogonadism (primary or hypogonadotropic)
Delayed puberty in select adolescent males
Palliative therapy for androgen-responsive metastatic breast cancer in women
dA: Topical gel 1%: start 50-81 mg once daily to clean dry skin; titrate 40.5-81 mg/day to serum testosterone
IM (cypionate/enanthate): 50-400 mg every 2-4 weeks (commonly 100-200 mg every 2 weeks)
Adjust to mid-normal serum testosterone; check trough before next dose
dP: Not routinely used in children; limited to delayed puberty in select adolescent boys under endocrinology.
dur: Chronic replacement with periodic monitoring (testosterone, hematocrit, PSA, lipids).
hl: Base ~10-100 min; cypionate ester ~8 days (IM depot).
se: Fluid retention and edema; increased blood pressure
ix: Warfarin — potentiates anticoagulant effect; monitor INR
Insulin / oral hypoglycemics — may lower glucose requirements
Corticosteroids — additive fluid retention and edema
ACTH — increased risk of edema
preg: Contraindicated in pregnancy; androgens can virilize a female fetus. Not recommended during breastfeeding.

uses: Healing and maintenance of erosive esophagitis
Prevention and healing of NSAID-associated gastric ulcers
dA: GERD/erosive esophagitis: 20-40 mg once daily, typically 4-8 weeks
H. pylori: 40 mg once daily with amoxicillin and clarithromycin
Zollinger-Ellison: 40 mg twice daily, titrated
Take 30-60 min before a meal
dP: Approved from age 1 month; 1-11 yr ~10 mg once daily; 12-17 yr 20-40 mg once daily
dur: 4-8 weeks for GERD/esophagitis; longer maintenance for erosive/hypersecretory disease.
ix: Clopidogrel — CYP2C19 inhibition reduces antiplatelet effect; avoid
Atazanavir/nelfinavir/rilpivirine — reduced absorption; contraindicated/avoid
Ketoconazole/itraconazole/iron/B12 — decreased absorption of pH-dependent drugs
High-dose methotrexate — increased levels/toxicity
Warfarin/digoxin — possible increased levels; monitor
preg: No clear increase in malformations; acceptable when needed. Small amounts in breast milk; use with caution.

uses: Short-term treatment of active duodenal ulcers
Maintenance to prevent duodenal ulcer recurrence
dA: Active duodenal ulcer: 1 g four times daily on an empty stomach (1 h before meals and at bedtime) for 4-8 weeks
Maintenance: 1 g twice daily
Take with water on an empty stomach; separate from antacids by 30 min
dP: Safety and efficacy not established in children; used off-label at weight-based doses under specialist guidance.
dur: 4-8 weeks for active ulcer; up to 1 year for maintenance.
ix: Fluoroquinolones — binds and reduces absorption; give quinolone 2 h before sucralfate
Levothyroxine — reduced absorption; separate by >=4 h
Phenytoin — decreased absorption; separate dosing and monitor
Digoxin/warfarin — reduced absorption; separate administration
preg: Minimal systemic absorption; commonly used for reflux/ulcer symptoms in pregnancy. Negligible milk transfer; compatible with breastfeeding.

uses: Symptomatic control of acute nonspecific diarrhea
Chronic diarrhea of inflammatory bowel disease
Reduction of stool volume in ileostomy

Rx (chronic/IBD): 4 mg initially then 2 mg per loose stool; max 16 mg/day
Discontinue if no improvement within 48 h in acute diarrhea
dP: Not for children under 2 years. Ages 2-5: only under physician guidance; older children reduced weight-based OTC dosing.
dur: Short-term for acute diarrhea; longer under supervision for chronic/IBD.
se: QT prolongation, torsades, cardiac arrest with high-dose/abuse
ix: CYP3A4/P-gp inhibitors (clarithromycin, ritonavir, quinidine) — raise levels and cardiac risk
QT-prolonging drugs — additive torsades risk at high doses
Gemfibrozil — increases loperamide levels
CNS depressants — additive sedation
preg: Generally acceptable for short-term use when needed, with caution. Small amounts in breast milk; short-term use usually compatible.

boxed: Contraindicated in children younger than 2 years — can cause fatal respiratory depression. Use the lowest effective dose with caution in children 2 years and older.
uses: Nausea and vomiting (postoperative, motion sickness, chemotherapy)
dA: Nausea/vomiting: 12.5-25 mg PO/IM/rectally every 4-6 h as needed
Allergy: 25 mg at bedtime or 12.5 mg before meals and at bedtime
Sedation: 25-50 mg per dose
Motion sickness: 25 mg 30-60 min before travel, then every 12 h
dP: Contraindicated under 2 years. Age 2+: 0.25-0.5 mg/kg (up to 12.5-25 mg) per dose; lowest effective dose.
dur: Short-term / as-needed; avoid prolonged or high-dose use.
se: Anticholinergic effects (dry mouth, blurred vision, urinary retention, constipation)
Severe tissue injury with IV extravasation
ix: CNS depressants (opioids, benzodiazepines, alcohol) — additive sedation and respiratory depression
Anticholinergics — additive dry mouth, retention, delirium
QT-prolonging drugs — increased arrhythmia risk
MAO inhibitors — enhanced anticholinergic/extrapyramidal effects
Epinephrine — reversed pressor effect
preg: Commonly used short-term for nausea/vomiting of pregnancy; avoid near delivery (neonatal respiratory/CNS depression). Excreted in breast milk; use caution (infant sedation).

boxed: Increased mortality in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis (antipsychotic class); not approved for dementia-related psychosis.
uses: Acute treatment of migraine (often IV/IM in the ED)
dA: Nausea/vomiting: 5-10 mg PO 3-4 times daily; max 40 mg/day
IM/IV: 5-10 mg (IV slowly, <=5 mg/min); may repeat q3-4h, max 40 mg/day
Rectal: 25 mg twice daily
Migraine (acute, off-label): 10 mg IV/IM, often with diphenhydramine to reduce akathisia/dystonia
dP: Children >=2 yr and >9 kg (nausea): weight-based 2.5 mg 1-3x/day (max 7.5-15 mg/day). Avoid <2 yr or <9 kg.
dur: Short-term/as-needed for nausea and migraine; chronic only for psychiatric use.
ix: CNS depressants — additive sedation and respiratory depression
Other QT-prolonging drugs — additive torsades risk
Anticholinergics — additive anticholinergic toxicity
Dopamine agonists/levodopa — mutual antagonism
Lithium — risk of neurotoxicity/encephalopathy
Epinephrine — do not use for drug-induced hypotension
preg: Use only if benefit justifies risk; third-trimester exposure may cause neonatal extrapyramidal/withdrawal symptoms. Distributed into breast milk; use caution.

uses: Induction of remission in mild-to-moderate ulcerative colitis
Maintenance of remission in ulcerative colitis
dA: Lialda: 2.4-4.8 g once daily with food for induction; 2.4 g once daily maintenance
Asacol HD: 1.6 g three times daily for active disease
Pentasa: 1 g four times daily (~4 g/day)
Rectal: 1 g suppository at bedtime or 4 g enema at bedtime for distal disease
dP: Some products studied in children >=5 yr, weight-based ~30-60 mg/kg/day divided (max ~4.8 g/day)
dur: Long-term maintenance therapy.
se: Acute intolerance syndrome (cramping, bloody diarrhea, fever, rash) mimicking a flare
ix: NSAIDs — additive nephrotoxicity/renal impairment
Nephrotoxic agents — increased renal injury risk
Azathioprine/6-mercaptopurine — increased myelosuppression
Antacids — may alter pH-dependent release of certain formulations
preg: Generally low-risk and often continued to maintain remission during pregnancy. Low amounts in breast milk; monitor the infant for diarrhea.

uses: Mild-to-moderate ulcerative colitis and maintenance of remission

Rheumatoid arthritis: 2 g/day (500 mg-1 g BID), titrated from 500 mg/day; max ~3 g/day
Take after meals with fluid; use enteric-coated tablets if GI intolerance
dP: JIA (>=6 yr): 30-50 mg/kg/day divided (max 2 g/day). UC (>=6 yr): initial 40-60 mg/kg/day divided; maintenance ~30 mg/kg/day
dur: Long-term maintenance therapy.
hl: Parent ~5.7-7.6 h; metabolite sulfapyridine ~5-10 h (longer in slow acetylators)
se: Blood dyscrasias: agranulocytosis, aplastic anemia (can be fatal)
ix: Folic acid — inhibits folate absorption (supplement folic acid)
Digoxin — decreased absorption and serum levels
Methotrexate — additive myelosuppression/hepatotoxicity
Azathioprine/6-mercaptopurine — increased myelosuppression
Warfarin — may potentiate anticoagulant effect
preg: Relatively safe and often continued in IBD/RA; supplement folic acid to reduce neural tube defect risk. Use caution in nursing; avoid in premature, ill, jaundiced, or G6PD-deficient infants.

boxed: Serious infections: increased risk of serious, sometimes fatal infections including tuberculosis (often disseminated), invasive fungal infections, and bacterial sepsis; test for latent TB before and during therapy.

Malignancy: lymphoma and other malignancies (some fatal) in children/adolescents; hepatosplenic T-cell lymphoma (usually fatal) reported mainly in adolescent/young-adult males with IBD, most on azathioprine or 6-mercaptopurine.
uses: Ankylosing spondylitis, psoriatic arthritis, plaque psoriasis
dA: Crohn's/UC: 5 mg/kg IV at weeks 0, 2, and 6, then every 8 weeks
May escalate to 10 mg/kg or shorten interval for inadequate response
Rheumatoid arthritis: 3 mg/kg IV at weeks 0, 2, 6, then every 8 weeks with methotrexate
dP: Pediatric Crohn's/UC (>=6 yr): 5 mg/kg IV at weeks 0, 2, 6, then every 8 weeks
dur: Chronic maintenance by IV infusion.
se: Anti-drug antibodies with loss of response
ix: Live vaccines — contraindicated (vaccinate before starting)
Anakinra — increased serious infections/neutropenia; do not combine
Abatacept/other biologic DMARDs — increased infection; avoid
Azathioprine/6-mercaptopurine — increased HSTCL risk
Narrow-index CYP substrates (warfarin, cyclosporine) — normalized inflammation may alter clearance

uses: Reduce risk of overt hepatic encephalopathy recurrence in adults
Travelers' diarrhea caused by noninvasive E. coli
dA: Hepatic encephalopathy: 550 mg twice daily
Travelers' diarrhea: 200 mg three times daily for 3 days
IBS-D: 550 mg three times daily for 14 days (may retreat up to twice)
dP: Travelers' diarrhea (>=12 yr): 200 mg three times daily for 3 days. Not routinely used in younger children.
dur: Course-based (3-14 days) for diarrhea; long-term for hepatic encephalopathy.
ix: Cyclosporine — increases rifaximin systemic exposure
Warfarin — reports of altered INR; monitor
P-glycoprotein inhibitors — may increase absorption
Otherwise minimal (negligible systemic absorption)
preg: Minimally absorbed; use only if clearly needed. Low milk transfer expected; use with caution.

dA: Pharyngitis: 500 mg PO 2-3 times daily or 250 mg PO 4 times daily x10 days
Mild-moderate infections: 250-500 mg PO every 6-8 h
Rheumatic fever prophylaxis: 250 mg PO twice daily
dP: Children <12 yr: 25-75 mg/kg/day divided every 6-8 h
Children >=12 yr: 250-500 mg PO 2-3 times daily x10 days for pharyngitis
dur: ~10 days for streptococcal pharyngitis; 7-14 days for other indications.
se: Black hairy tongue and oral candidiasis
ix: Probenecid — decreases renal clearance, raising penicillin levels
Methotrexate — reduced clearance, increased toxicity
Oral contraceptives — possible reduced efficacy
Tetracyclines — may antagonize penicillin activity
preg: Considered safe in pregnancy. Small amounts in breast milk; generally compatible (monitor infant for rash/diarrhea/candidiasis).

uses: Bacterial meningitis, including Listeria and susceptible gram-negatives
Urinary tract infections from susceptible organisms

IV/IM: 1-2 g every 4-6 h for moderate-severe infections
Meningitis: 2 g IV every 4 h (150-200 mg/kg/day)
Enterococcal endocarditis: 2 g IV every 4 h with gentamicin
