IV/IM: 100-200 mg/kg/day divided q6h; meningitis 200-400 mg/kg/day divided q4-6h
dur: 7-14 days typical; 14-21 days for meningitis.
se: Rare interstitial nephritis or hematologic effects
ix: Probenecid — decreases renal clearance, increasing levels

Topical or other carbonic anhydrase inhibitors — additive systemic acidosis, avoid combining
Lithium — increases renal lithium excretion, lowering lithium levels
Digoxin — acetazolamide-induced hypokalemia potentiates digitalis toxicity
Other drugs affected by urine alkalinization (amphetamines, quinidine) — altered clearance
preg: Former FDA Category C; teratogenic in animals at high doses and generally avoided, especially in the first trimester unless benefit outweighs risk. Excreted in breast milk in small amounts; use caution while nursing.

uses: Reduction of elevated intracranial pressure and cerebral edema
Promotion of diuresis in acute kidney injury (oliguria) prevention
Promotion of urinary excretion of toxic substances
Irrigation solution during transurethral procedures (lower concentrations)
dA: Increased ICP / cerebral edema: 0.25–1 g/kg IV as a 15–25% solution infused over 30–60 min; may repeat every 6–8 h
Test dose for oliguria: 0.2 g/kg IV over 3–5 min; general diuresis 50–100 g IV
Maintain serum osmolality below ~320 mOsm/kg to limit renal risk
dP: Increased ICP / cerebral edema: 0.25–1 g/kg IV per dose over 30–60 min; may repeat every 6–8 h as needed
Debilitated or small pediatric patients: 0.5 g/kg may be sufficient
dur: Diuresis begins within 1–3 h; intracranial/intraocular pressure falls within ~15 min and lasts 3–8 h.
se: Pulmonary edema / fluid overload (especially in CHF)
Dehydration and hypotension with excessive diuresis
Acute kidney injury with high cumulative doses
Infusion-site phlebitis; crystallization at low temperatures
ix: Nephrotoxic drugs (aminoglycosides, cyclosporine, NSAIDs) — additive renal injury
Other diuretics — enhanced diuretic and electrolyte-depleting effect
Digoxin — mannitol-induced hypokalemia increases digoxin toxicity risk
Neurotoxic agents (e.g., aminoglycosides) — increased CNS penetration/toxicity
preg: Former FDA Category C; crosses the placenta and adequate human data are lacking, so use only if clearly needed. It is unknown whether mannitol is excreted in breast milk; use caution during lactation.

uses: Overactive bladder with urge urinary incontinence, urgency, and frequency
Neurogenic detrusor overactivity in pediatric patients (≥3 yr)
Often combined with an antimuscarinic (e.g., solifenacin) for refractory OAB
dA: Overactive bladder: 25 mg orally once daily; may increase to 50 mg once daily after 8 weeks
Severe renal or moderate hepatic impairment: do not exceed 25 mg once daily
Take with or without food; swallow ER tablet whole
dP: Neurogenic detrusor overactivity (≥3 yr, ≥35 kg): 25 mg ER tablet daily, up to 50 mg
Weight-based oral granules for children ≥3 yr weighing <35 kg
dur: Steady state reached in ~7 days; symptom improvement may take up to 8 weeks. Once-daily dosing.
se: Urinary retention (especially with bladder outlet obstruction or antimuscarinics)
Rare angioedema of face, lips, tongue
ix: Metoprolol and other CYP2D6 substrates — mirabegron inhibits CYP2D6, raising their levels
Digoxin — increased digoxin concentration; use lowest digoxin dose and monitor
Desipramine / other narrow-index CYP2D6 drugs — increased exposure
Antimuscarinics (e.g., solifenacin) — additive urinary retention risk
preg: Limited human data; animal studies showed adverse effects at high doses, so use in pregnancy only if clearly needed. Not recommended during breastfeeding because mirabegron is excreted in the milk of animals.

boxed: Can cause abortion, premature birth, or birth defects; may cause uterine rupture (risk rises with gestational age and prior uterine surgery, including cesarean). Must NOT be used to reduce NSAID-induced ulcer risk in women who are pregnant.
uses: Treatment and prevention of postpartum hemorrhage from uterine atony (off-label)
Management of missed abortion and incomplete miscarriage
dA: NSAID ulcer prevention: 200 mcg orally 4 times daily with food (reduce to 100 mcg QID if not tolerated)
Postpartum hemorrhage: 800–1000 mcg rectally, or 600–800 mcg sublingual/buccal, single dose
Cervical ripening/labor induction: 25 mcg intravaginally every 3–6 h
Medical abortion: 800 mcg buccally/vaginally 24–48 h after mifepristone
dP: Not routinely used in children.
dur: Onset within minutes; uterotonic effect lasts several hours. For ulcer prophylaxis, continue for the duration of NSAID therapy.
se: Fever and chills (dose-related, common with obstetric use)
ix: Magnesium-containing antacids — worsen misoprostol-induced diarrhea
Oxytocin / other uterotonics — additive uterine stimulation and tachysystole risk
NSAIDs — no significant pharmacokinetic interaction but is the drug misoprostol protects against
Food/antacids — reduce absorption rate and peak levels
preg: Contraindicated in pregnancy when used for ulcer prevention because it causes abortion, birth defects, premature birth, and uterine rupture. Small amounts of misoprostol acid pass into breast milk; brief exposure for postpartum/obstetric single doses is generally considered compatible with breastfeeding.

uses: Prevention and treatment of postpartum hemorrhage from uterine atony or subinvolution
Control of uterine bleeding after delivery of the placenta
Promotion of uterine involution during the puerperium
dA: 0.2 mg IM after delivery of the placenta or during the puerperium; may repeat every 2–4 h as needed
Severe hemorrhage: 0.2 mg slow IV over ≥60 s with BP monitoring (reserved for emergencies)
Maintenance: 0.2 mg orally 3–4 times daily for up to 1 week during the puerperium
dP: Not routinely used in children.
dur: IM onset 2–5 min (lasting ~3 h); oral onset 5–10 min. Continue oral therapy up to 7 days postpartum as needed.
se: Rare seizures or stroke with hypertensive crisis
ix: Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (macrolides, azole antifungals, protease inhibitors) — risk of severe vasospasm/hypertension, contraindicated
Triptans and ergot alkaloids — additive vasoconstriction, contraindicated
Other vasoconstrictors/sympathomimetics — potentiated hypertension
Beta-blockers — enhanced peripheral vasoconstriction
preg: Contraindicated during pregnancy and before delivery because it causes strong uterine contractions and fetal harm. Avoid breastfeeding for about 12 hours after a dose (discard milk expressed during that window) because ergot alkaloids pass into milk.

boxed: Anaphylaxis: risk of severe hypersensitivity reactions including anaphylaxis; discontinue permanently if they occur
Hemolysis in patients with G6PD deficiency: contraindicated; screen high-risk patients (e.g., of African or Mediterranean ancestry) before starting
Methemoglobinemia: can cause serious hypoxemia; discontinue permanently
Interference with uric acid measurements: enzymatic degradation of uric acid in blood samples at room temperature causes spuriously low readings; collect samples in pre-chilled heparin tubes on ice
uses: Management and prevention of hyperuricemia from tumor lysis syndrome
Given with chemotherapy in leukemia, lymphoma, and solid tumor malignancies at high risk of TLS
Rapidly lowers plasma uric acid in patients with elevated or expected-to-rise levels
dA: 0.2 mg/kg IV once daily infused over 30 minutes for up to 5 days
Duration and repeat courses individualized to uric acid levels and clinical judgment
dP: Children 1 month-17 years: 0.2 mg/kg IV once daily over 30 minutes for up to 5 days
dur: Up to 5 days; a single course (no more than one) is recommended.
ix: Minimal drug-drug interactions — does not meaningfully inhibit/induce CYP enzymes
Blood uric acid assays — degrades urate ex vivo causing falsely low results unless samples are chilled
Oxidant drugs — may add to methemoglobinemia/hemolysis risk in susceptible patients
Allopurinol — no clinically significant interaction, but combined use is generally unnecessary
preg: Limited human data; animal studies are lacking, so use in pregnancy only if clearly needed (former Category C). It is unknown whether rasburicase passes into breast milk; a decision to discontinue nursing or the drug should weigh benefit to the mother.

uses: Relief of inflammation and itching in corticosteroid-responsive dermatoses
Scalp psoriasis and seborrheic dermatitis (foam/shampoo/solution forms)
dA: Apply a thin film to affected skin twice daily and rub in gently
Limit to 2 consecutive weeks; do not exceed 50 g (or 50 mL) per week
Discontinue when control is achieved; avoid occlusion and use on face, groin, or axillae
dP: Not recommended under 12 years of age; children are more susceptible to HPA-axis suppression and systemic toxicity
dur: Maximum 2 weeks continuous use (up to 4 weeks for scalp with strict limits); ≤50 g/week.
hl: Not clinically characterized for topical use (minimal systemic absorption with intact skin)
se: Burning, stinging, itching, or irritation at application site
Skin atrophy, thinning, striae, and telangiectasia
HPA-axis suppression / Cushing syndrome / hyperglycemia with extensive or prolonged use
Skin infection or delayed wound healing
ix: Other systemic corticosteroids — additive risk of HPA-axis suppression
Occlusive dressings — increase absorption and systemic/local toxicity
CYP3A4 inhibitors (e.g., ritonavir, itraconazole) — may raise systemic corticosteroid exposure
Live vaccines — theoretical reduced response with significant systemic absorption
preg: Systemic absorption is generally low, but corticosteroids can be teratogenic in animals; use the smallest amount for the shortest time during pregnancy and avoid extensive application. It is unknown whether topical clobetasol enters breast milk, so avoid applying to the chest area before nursing.

uses: Topical treatment of acne vulgaris (comedones, papules, pustules)
Reduces formation of new comedones and promotes keratolysis
Photodamage: mitigation of fine wrinkles, mottled hyperpigmentation, roughness (Renova)
dA: Apply a pea-sized amount to the entire affected area once daily at bedtime
Apply to clean, dry skin; start with lower strength and space applications if irritation occurs
Use sunscreen and limit sun exposure during treatment
dP: Children ≥12 years: same as adult acne dosing — thin application once nightly; safety in younger children not established
dur: Chronic/long-term nightly use; therapeutic response typically after 6-12 weeks.
hl: Not clinically relevant with topical use (negligible systemic absorption)
se: Burning, stinging, or warmth after application
Transient worsening ("purging") of acne early in treatment
ix: Topical benzoyl peroxide — can oxidize/inactivate tretinoin if applied at the same time
Other topical drying/irritant agents (sulfur, resorcinol, salicylic acid) — additive irritation
Photosensitizing drugs (e.g., thiazides, fluoroquinolones, tetracyclines) — additive sun sensitivity
Astringents/medicated cosmetics — increased local irritation
preg: Topical tretinoin has limited systemic absorption and no clear proof of human teratogenicity, but retinoids raise theoretical concern, so it is generally avoided in pregnancy unless clearly needed. It is unknown whether it passes into breast milk; avoid applying to the nipple/areola when nursing.

uses: Lowers intraocular pressure in open-angle glaucoma
dA: 1 drop of 0.25% in the affected eye(s) twice daily; increase to 0.5% if response is inadequate
Gel-forming solution (Timoptic-XE) or Istalol: 1 drop once daily in the morning
Once controlled, some patients maintained on 0.25% or 0.5% once daily
dP: Safety and efficacy in children not fully established; used cautiously by specialists (e.g., pediatric/congenital glaucoma) with careful monitoring for systemic beta-blockade
dur: Chronic, indefinite daily use with periodic IOP monitoring.
hl: Systemic plasma half-life approximately 4 hours after ocular absorption
se: Bronchospasm/dyspnea, especially in asthma or COPD
Depression or masking of hypoglycemia symptoms
ix: Systemic beta-blockers — additive systemic beta-blockade and bradycardia
Calcium channel blockers (verapamil, diltiazem) — additive hypotension, bradycardia, AV block
Digoxin — additive slowing of AV conduction and bradycardia
Oral CYP2D6 inhibitors (e.g., quinidine, SSRIs) — increased systemic timolol levels/effects
Clonidine — potentiated rebound hypertension on withdrawal
preg: Systemic exposure occurs from ocular absorption; data are limited, so use in pregnancy only if the benefit justifies risk, and nasolacrimal occlusion can reduce systemic uptake. Timolol is excreted in breast milk, so caution is advised while nursing.

uses: Relief of seasonal allergic rhinitis symptoms
Treatment of chronic idiopathic urticaria (itching and hives)
dA: 180 mg orally once daily, or 60 mg twice daily
Renal impairment: 60 mg once daily
Take with water, not fruit juice
dP: Children 2-11 years: 30 mg twice daily (oral suspension/tablet)
Chronic urticaria 6 months-2 years: 15 mg twice daily; ≥12 years: adult dosing
dur: As needed for symptom control; may be used chronically for persistent allergy/urticaria.
ix: Aluminum/magnesium antacids — reduce fexofenadine absorption; separate by at least 2 hours
Apple, orange, or grapefruit juice — decrease bioavailability via OATP inhibition
Erythromycin — raises fexofenadine plasma concentrations
Ketoconazole — raises fexofenadine plasma concentrations
preg: Human data are limited but there is no clear evidence of harm; use in pregnancy only if clearly needed (former Category C). Small amounts may pass into breast milk, but it is generally considered compatible with breastfeeding at usual doses.

uses: Acceleration of fetal lung maturity in anticipated preterm birth (24–34 weeks gestation)
Reduces neonatal respiratory distress syndrome, intraventricular hemorrhage, and mortality
Anti-inflammatory/immunosuppressive therapy for allergic, rheumatic, and dermatologic disease
dA: Antenatal: 12 mg IM every 24 hours for 2 doses (fetal lung maturity)
A single rescue course may be considered if delivery is still anticipated ≥7 days after the initial course
Non-obstetric: 0.5–9 mg/day IM depending on indication
dP: Antenatal dosing is given to the mother, not the neonate
Systemic pediatric use: individualized by weight/BSA and disease; use lowest effective dose
dur: Antenatal: 2 doses over 24 hours; benefit greatest if delivery occurs 24 hours to 7 days after first dose
hl: Plasma half-life ~5–6 hours; biologic (tissue) effect 36–54 hours (long-acting)
se: Transient fetal heart rate and movement changes
ix: Live vaccines — reduced response and risk of disseminated infection
CYP3A4 inducers (rifampin, phenytoin) — reduced corticosteroid effect
Potassium-depleting diuretics — additive hypokalemia
NSAIDs — increased GI ulceration risk
Antidiabetic agents — reduced glycemic control (hyperglycemia)
preg: Used intentionally in pregnancy for fetal lung maturation; benefits outweigh risks in threatened preterm birth. Small amounts enter breast milk but antenatal single-course use is considered compatible with breastfeeding.

boxed: Should NOT be used for prolonged tocolysis (beyond 48–72 hours) because of the potential for serious maternal cardiac events and death
Should NOT be used in outpatient or home settings, or with oral terbutaline for maintenance tocolysis, due to lack of efficacy and serious maternal adverse events
uses: Acute, short-term tocolysis to inhibit preterm uterine contractions (in-hospital, <48–72 h)
Relief of bronchospasm in asthma and reversible obstructive airway disease
Uterine relaxation for intrapartum emergencies (e.g., tachysystole, cord prolapse, external version)
dA: Acute tocolysis: 0.25 mg subcutaneously every 20–30 min, up to 3 doses (hold for maternal HR >120 bpm)
Bronchospasm: 0.25 mg SC, may repeat once in 15–30 min (max 0.5 mg/4 h)
Oral (bronchospasm): 2.5–5 mg PO every 6–8 hours (max 15 mg/day)
dP: Bronchospasm (≥12 yr): as adult SC/oral dosing
Not routinely used for tocolysis in children
dur: Tocolysis is acute/short-term only (<48–72 hours); prolonged or outpatient use is contraindicated by boxed warning
hl: Terminal half-life ~3–4 hours (reported range up to ~14 hours)
se: Pulmonary edema (especially with prolonged tocolysis or fluid overload)
ix: Other sympathomimetics — additive cardiovascular toxicity (not recommended)
Beta-blockers — mutual antagonism; may cause severe bronchospasm
MAO inhibitors / tricyclic antidepressants — potentiated vascular/cardiac effects
Non-potassium-sparing diuretics — additive hypokalemia and ECG changes
Digoxin — increased arrhythmia risk with hypokalemia
preg: Used short-term in pregnancy for acute tocolysis but carries a boxed warning against prolonged/outpatient use due to maternal death and cardiac events. Excreted in breast milk in small amounts; generally considered compatible with breastfeeding.

uses: Palliative treatment of advanced prostate cancer
Management of endometriosis pain (with or without add-back therapy)
Preoperative shrinkage of uterine fibroids and treatment of anemia from fibroids
dA: Endometriosis/fibroids: Lupron Depot 3.75 mg IM monthly, or 11.25 mg IM every 3 months (max 6 months per course)
Prostate cancer: Lupron Depot 7.5 mg IM monthly, 22.5 mg q3mo, 30 mg q4mo, or 45 mg q6mo
Eligard SC formulations: 7.5 mg monthly up to 45 mg q6mo
dP: Central precocious puberty: Fensolvi 45 mg SC every 6 months, or weight-based Lupron Depot-PED IM monthly, titrated to suppress puberty
Not used for endometriosis/fibroids/prostate cancer in children
dur: Endometriosis/fibroids limited to 6 months per course (bone loss); prostate cancer and precocious puberty continued long-term as indicated
hl: Terminal elimination half-life ~3 hours; depot provides sustained suppression over dosing interval
se: Mood changes, decreased libido, vaginal dryness / erectile dysfunction
QT prolongation, hyperglycemia, and cardiovascular risk with androgen deprivation
ix: QT-prolonging drugs (antiarrhythmics, certain antipsychotics) — additive QT prolongation
Antidiabetic agents — androgen deprivation may worsen glycemic control
Drugs affecting pituitary gonadotropins — may reduce therapeutic suppression
Hyperglycemia-inducing agents — additive metabolic effects
preg: Contraindicated in pregnancy (Category X); may cause fetal harm and pregnancy loss—exclude pregnancy before starting and use non-hormonal contraception. Not recommended during breastfeeding.

boxed: Fatal infusion-related reactions (most within 24 hours of first infusion)
Severe, sometimes fatal, mucocutaneous reactions (e.g., Stevens-Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis)
Hepatitis B virus reactivation, which can cause fulminant hepatitis, hepatic failure, and death
Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML), including fatal PML
uses: CD20-positive non-Hodgkin lymphoma (alone or with chemotherapy)
Moderate-to-severe rheumatoid arthritis (with methotrexate) after TNF-inhibitor failure
Granulomatosis with polyangiitis and microscopic polyangiitis
dA: NHL: 375 mg/m² IV weekly for 4 doses, or per chemotherapy protocol
CLL: 375 mg/m² day before FC cycle 1, then 500 mg/m² on day 1 of cycles 2–6
Rheumatoid arthritis: two 1000 mg IV infusions 2 weeks apart, repeated every ≥24 weeks
GPA/MPA: 375 mg/m² IV weekly for 4 weeks (induction)
dP: Pediatric NHL/mature B-cell leukemia: 375 mg/m² IV per protocol with chemotherapy
Pediatric GPA/MPA: 375 mg/m² IV weekly for 4 weeks
dur: Course/cycle-based by indication; premedicate to reduce infusion reactions and screen for HBV before starting
hl: Terminal half-life variable, averaging ~18–22 days (range roughly days to weeks depending on tumor burden and dose)
se: Increased risk of serious bacterial, viral, and fungal infections
ix: Live vaccines — avoid; impaired immune response and infection risk
Other immunosuppressants/biologics — additive immunosuppression and infection risk
Cisplatin — renal toxicity (not an approved combination)
Antihypertensives — may worsen infusion-related hypotension (hold before infusion)
preg: Can cause fetal B-cell depletion; avoid in pregnancy and use effective contraception during and for 12 months after therapy. Breastfeeding not recommended during and for ~6 months after the last dose.

boxed: Severe myelosuppression—monitor blood counts; may cause life-threatening anemia, neutropenia, and thrombocytopenia
Carcinogenic—associated with secondary malignancies, including leukemia and skin cancers, with long-term use
uses: Reduces frequency of painful crises and need for transfusions in sickle cell anemia
Chronic myeloid leukemia and other myeloproliferative neoplasms (cytoreduction)
Radiosensitizer for head and neck squamous cell carcinoma
Control of thrombocytosis/leukocytosis in polycythemia vera and essential thrombocythemia
dA: Sickle cell disease: start 15 mg/kg/day PO once daily; titrate by 5 mg/kg/day every 8–12 weeks to max tolerated dose (usually up to 35 mg/kg/day)
Chronic myeloproliferative disease: 15–30 mg/kg/day PO, adjusted to counts
Hold and reduce dose for myelosuppression (ANC/platelet thresholds)
dP: Sickle cell disease (Siklos, ≥2 years or per label ≥9 months): 20 mg/kg/day once daily, titrated by 5 mg/kg/day every 8 weeks to max 35 mg/kg/day, monitoring counts
dur: Long-term chronic therapy in sickle cell disease and myeloproliferative disorders, with ongoing CBC monitoring
ix: Antiretrovirals (didanosine ± stavudine) — pancreatitis, hepatotoxicity, peripheral neuropathy (fatal cases); avoid
Other myelosuppressive agents / radiation — additive marrow suppression
Live vaccines — risk of severe disseminated infection; avoid
Uricosurics/allopurinol interplay — hyperuricemia may require management
Interference with uric acid, urea, and lactic acid assays
preg: Contraindicated/avoid in pregnancy—can cause fetal harm; both females and males of reproductive potential should use effective contraception during and after therapy. Excreted in breast milk; discontinue breastfeeding during treatment.
